utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We shall read this as soon as the Registry will have handed over the copies to us. Mr. Scott, you now officially have the floor to give us an overall view of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please the Court, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel. It is time, gentlemen, that we take the opportunity to gather the Croatian people inside the broadest, widest possible borders. On the 27th of December, 1991, in Zagreb, Croatia's then president, Franjo Tudjman, told an assembled group of Croat and Bosnian Croat leaders: "The State of Croatia cannot survive such as it is, but a Croatian State, even within the borders of the banovina could, not to mention if these borders were improved on." "It seems to me, therefore, that just as we have taken advantage of this historic moment to establish an independent, internationally recognised Croatia, I believe that it is time that we take the opportunity to gather the Croatian people inside the widest possible borders ..." Turning to the 4th of August, 1993, a woman who we'll call, for today's purposes, Samira, she must have started that day like many other days --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you speak into the microphone, Mr. Scott, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm afraid not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On the 27th of December, 1991, Your Honours, Franjo Tudjman said that it was time to gather the Croatian people inside the widest possible borders. Moving ahead to the 4th of August, 1993, a woman who we will call Samira must have started that day like any other day during that time. Probably with some anxiety about what had already happened in the previous days, what was going on in her area where she lived, but without any reason to know that on that particular day what would happen to her and her children and her elderly mother. By that day, the 4th of August, her husband had already been arrested and taken away by HVO soldiers, Muslim houses in her area had been burned, several mosques had been destroyed, and Muslim women were being mistreated. But then on the 4th of August, 1993, her world was turned even more upside-down. HVO soldiers came to Samira's house and gave Samira, her children, and her elderly mother five minutes to leave the home. They were then taken to a collection point in Stolac and detained there with 400 other Muslim women and children. HVO soldiers robbed them of their valuables and they were then expelled from Stolac municipality altogether, when the HVO took them in vehicles to Buna, south of Mostar, and told the women and children to walk, under gunfire, in the direction of Blagaj. By September of 1993, Your Honours, all of the Muslims had been expelled from Stolac municipality. One might be inclined to describe such behaviour, such violence as senseless, and it surely was in the sense of being without any real justification. But on the other hand, in another sense, it was not senseless at all, because it was based on a sense of things, however misguided or wrong, and was done with a purpose. In short, it was not senseless, it was purposeful and plainly foreseeable. To see this, we must only look at the words of President Tudjman and others around this same time, September 1993. On the 21st of September, President Tudjman told a group of Croat and Bosnian Croat leaders: "Stolac. I know the strategic importance of Stolac, both as the president of Croatia and, if you will, as a soldier. I know that Stolac and the entire former Jablanicki Kotar and Konjic were included in the Croatian Banovina in 1939. These are arguments I have upheld since the first day." At the same meeting, a Bosnian Croat leader proudly reported to Tudjman: "Today there is not a single Muslim in Stolac. We have populated Stolac with our refugees from Bosnia." To which Tudjman responded, "... I know all that. I know all that." It is good, Your Honour, to start by looking at the words of the indictment in connection with the charges in this case, in connection with the joint criminal enterprise that is charged, which is stated in paragraph 15 of the indictment. And we need a technical moment here, Your Honour. The technical systems do not seem to be functioning very well today, Your Honour, I'm afraid. Now we have it. Paragraph 15 of the indictment: "From on or before the 18th of November, 1991, to about April 1994 and thereafter, various persons established and participated in a joint criminal enterprise to politically and militarily subjugate, permanently remove and ethnically cleanse Bosnian Muslims and other non-Croats who lived in areas on the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina which were claimed to be part of the Croatian Community (and later Republic) of Herceg-Bosna, and to join these areas as part of a 'Greater Croatia,' whether in the short run or over time and whether as part of the Republic of Croatia or in close association with it, by force, fear, or threat of force, persecution, imprisonment and detention, forcible transfer and deportation, appropriation and destruction of property and other means, which constituted or involved the commission of crimes which are punishable under Articles 2, 3, and 5 of the Tribunal Statute. The territorial ambition of this joint criminal enterprise, Mr. President, Your Honours, was to establish a Croatian territory with the borders of the Croatian Banovina, a territorial entity that existed from 1939 to 1941. It was part of the joint criminal enterprise to engineer the political and ethnic map of these areas so that they would be Croat-dominated, both politically and demographically." Now, in terms of the membership or the make-up of this joint criminal enterprise and those who assisted it, we can look at paragraphs 16, and 16.1 of the indictment, which states that: "A number of persons joined, participated in and contributed to the joint criminal enterprise, including Franjo Tudjman, the President of the Republic of Croatia -" who is deceased - "Mr. Gojko Susak, the minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia, (deceased...); Janko Bobetko, a senior general in the army of the Republic of Croatia, (deceased ...); Mate Boban, the president of the Croatian Community (and later Republic) of Herceg-Bosna, (deceased ...); Jadranko Prlic; Bruno Stojic; Slobodan Praljak; Milivoj Petkovic; Valentin Coric; Berislav Pusic; Dario Kordic; Tihomir Blaskic; Mladen Naletilic (also known as 'Tuta') and others." These persons planned, prepared and implemented the objectives of the joint criminal enterprise together, in other words, as members of or participants in the enterprise and or through as agents or instruments, either directly or indirectly, members of the Croatian Community or Republic of Herceg-Bosna, the Croatian Defence Council or HVO, and the leadership and authorities of those bodies, including various officials and members of the government and political structures at all levels, as well as leaders and members of the Croatian Democratic Union, a political party, and the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Bosnian branch, if you will, of the party in Zagreb, at all levels, various officers and members of the Herceg-Bosna HVO forces, and various members of the armed forces, police, security and intelligence services of the Republic of Croatia and other persons both known and unknown. Your Honours, the events charged in this case occurred as part of the dissolution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. During or about this time, in 1989, Franjo Tudjman and others formed a political party in Croatia called the Croatian Democratic Union, or HDZ. Tudjman was elected president of Croatia in 1990 and remained in this position as president of the country until he died in December 1999. The Republic of Croatia declared its existence -- or, excuse me, its independence from Yugoslavia on the 25th of June, 1991, and by September of 1991, the Republic of Croatia was at war with nationalist Serb forces attempting to incorporate parts of Croatia into a Greater Serbia. The European Community recognised the Republic of Croatia as an independent state on the 15th of January, 1992, and the United Nations admitted Croatia as a member state on the 22nd of May, 1992. The evidence will show, Your Honours, that long before the HDZ came into existence, Franjo Tudjman had given voice to his views concerning Croatia's acquisition of, or rights to certain parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As early as 1981, Tudjman, in his own published work, described Bosnia and Croatia as a "indivisible geographic and economic entity." He advocated and supported Croatia's claims to large parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina which had been part of the Croatian Banovina, a territorial and administrative entity agreed to by Croats -- Croat and Serb leaders in 1939. With the dissolution of Yugoslavia, both Serbia and Croatia saw opportunities for territorial expansion in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Discussions aimed toward the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina were held between Franjo Tudjman and Slobodan Milosevic at Karadjordjevo in Serbia in March of 1991, and were initially so successful - at least, Franjo Tudjman thought they were so successful - that he thought that he and Milosevic could "solve" the reorganisation of Yugoslavia, including the division or partition of Bosnia without Milosevic being a military threat to Croatia. Indeed, on the eve of Croatia breaking free of Yugoslavia, Tudjman made his ambitions toward Bosnian territory clear at a meeting of the Supreme State Council of Croatia on the 8th of June, 1991. Tudjman said: "... if we opt for Croatia's independence, either within an alliance or total independence, Croatia's borders, such as they are today, are absurd, they are impossible, in the sense of administration and trade, let alone as regards any kind of protection of these borders of Croatia. Therefore, from our point of view no less than from the Serbian, there is the problem of - there is a need to find an essential solution to the problem, isn't that so, because the establishment of Bosnia, the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina after World War II are historically absurd ..." We'll start by showing, just by way of overall orientation, a map of the former Yugoslavia showing the -- showing both Serbia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and some of the main cities and towns -- or towns in those areas to give the Court a general overview of the region that we're talking about. Of course, toward the upper left-hand portion of the screen we see the capital of Croatia, Zagreb. Toward approximately the middle part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, you see the city of Sarajevo; and to the south of Sarajevo you see the city of Mostar, a city which will feature prominently throughout this case and in which the Bosnian Croats -- which the Herceg-Bosna leadership declared the capital of Herceg-Bosna. Tudjman was clear in his view that the survival of Bosnia and Herzegovina, at least in the form that then existed, was against Croatia's interest. He said on the 27th of December, 1991, meeting: "The survival of Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent and sovereign state, even if possible, is in any case against the interests of the Croatian state and makes impossible the normal territorial establishment of the Croatian state and creates conditions for the disappearance of what remains of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina today. "All of history has shown that Bosnia and Herzegovina is no solution for the Croatian people." "Bosnia and Herzegovina should not be taken as something God given which must be preserved, and we must especially not forget how harmful it is. Because of the creation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia has been put in an impossible situation regarding its territory." Later in that same meeting, a very important meeting which the Chamber will hear evidence of, the leadership of the Bosnian Croats, the leadership of Tudjman and his close associates in that meeting where all these things were discussed, Tudjman said, made the statement which I referred to earlier: The State of Croatia could not survive within its current borders but within the banovina it very well could, or indeed those borders might even be improved on. And it was at that meeting at that time that Tudjman made the statement: "... I believe that it is time that we take the opportunity to gather the Croatian people inside the widest possible borders ..." Tudjman told his senior advisors in late 1992 that "on the Bosnia and Herzegovina question," we have stated in the preamble to the Croatian Constitution "that the preservation of Croatian statehood implies also the Croatian Banovina." On the 17th of September, 1992, Tudjman said: "Therefore, on ... this question, we have stated in the preface, or as lawyers say, the preamble, to the Croatian constitution, one point: That the preservation of Croatian statehood implies also the Croatian Banovina. This remark was not lightly made, or on the spur of a moment, or just in passing, but rather on the basis of the assessment of the totality of historical facts, after long discussions of this nature in smaller or larger circles." Now, I've mentioned, Your Honour, so far several times the Croatian Banovina of 1939, and what we've now put on the display is a map showing the borders of the banovina as they existed at that time. And as you will see, not only on the existing borders or existing territory of Croatia but then - and various places will become clear in a moment - reaching well into the centre of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This next map is a -- simply a map of Bosnia and Herzegovina showing the municipalities. Some might call them counties or states or municipalities or opstinas, but these are the subdivisions of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina as they existed in 1991. If you go to the next slide. Now you will see the overlay of the banovina on Bosnia and Herzegovina. And these were the territorial claims made by Croatia, made by Tudjman and others, and you will see the borders of those claims outlined in red reaching far into Central Bosnia from the south, and also in the upper northern side of the country you will also see the borders of the banovina encroaching into Bosnia and Herzegovina. At this moment, Your Honours, we would like to play the first clip. If we could have the assistance of the technical booth, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Only a few days after the 17th of September, 1992, meeting, Tudjman again made it clear that the territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina that was within the banovina was part of Croatia and that the Bosnian government, the government of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, could make no claim - I repeat - could make no claim to any part of it. Tudjman said: "There exist worrying developments, desires, to take control even over those areas, in those Croatian areas that the HVO -" that is, the Croatian Defence Council - "liberated and has power." "We will openly tell Izetbegovic --" the president of Bosnia. "We will openly tell Izetbegovic when he comes here what we said in the beginning. There can be no discussion about them establishing military and civilian government in areas that used to be within the Croatian Banovina." At which point Defence Minister Gojko Susak added: "... the Croats would never allow Muslims to form military units in Mostar, Capljina and Stolac, saying that the Croats had already 'liberated' these areas." Now, we have some adjudicated facts that have been established by other Tribunal judgements that the Chamber, with all respect, we believe, should take note of. Adjudicated fact number 77 as found by the Trial Chamber: "President Tudjman, as the leader of the HDZ, sought to promote a Croatian identity by appealing to Croatia as a distinct and historically continuous entity." Adjudicated fact number 81: "The view that President Tudjman harboured territorial ambitions in respect of Bosnia and Herzegovina, despite his official position to the contrary, is strengthened by reports of discussions held between Tudjman and Milosevic against the backdrop of the break-up of the Yugoslav federation in 1991." It might be noted before we go on that the model, if you will, or the concept of the banovina was not the only territorial precedent that Franjo Tudjman and others might have appealed to. Although revival, for example, of the World War II borders of the Independent State of Croatia was advocated by some, it held no appeal for Tudjman since it included too many non-Croats. Tudjman said again on the 17th of September, he told Mate Boban and including Jadranko Prlic, who sits in this courtroom, on the 17th of September, 1992: "And you know, even if they gave us, we must be alert, if they gave us a border on the Drina with two million Muslims and one and a half million Serbs, whose state would that be?" Having said this, the fact that substantial parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina that Tudjman encompassed within the banovina were Muslim-majority or Muslim-plurality areas did not stop him from claiming those areas. Tudjman told a group of Herzegovina representatives in September 1993, in connection with the HVO having taken control of Stolac municipality and by September of 1993 having expelled every Muslim from the municipality, "I know the importance of Stolac, and I have made these arguments since the first day." Now, if you look, by way of orientation on the map, you will see Stolac down toward the bottom part of the map of the country. If you find Mostar, Stolac is the municipality immediately to the south of Mostar, again almost in the bottom part of the map there. That will show you the municipality of Stolac within the borders of the banovina. Now, the problem with Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I say the problem, it's a problem from the perspective of anyone trying to divide up the country into a small number of largely homogenous ethnic or national groups, the problem is that Bosnia and Herzegovina, in 1990 and 1991, was comprised of the various ethnic groups spread out all over the country, in larger and smaller pockets and enclaves, making a demographic map of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1991 look like, as has been famously described, leopard spots. If you look at the map that is now on the display, map number 9, you will get a sense of the ethnic composition of Bosnia and Herzegovina as it existed in 1991. And you'll see that in virtually -- while there are some predominant areas where one ethnic group may have been in a majority, you will see that throughout the country from corner to corner, from border to border, there were Muslims everywhere, there were Croats everywhere, there were Serbs everywhere. You can see the same thing in a map showing the demographic -- demographic characteristics of the municipality of Mostar. In this map you will see that the Croat areas are marked in red, the Serb areas in blue, and the Muslim areas in green. Once again, you see even in one municipality the intermixture of the various ethnic and national groups. And indeed the Tribunal's already established this basic fact in adjudicated fact number 10: "Bosnia, in addition to hosting the most ethnically diverse population, was unique among the republics -" that is the republics of the former Yugoslavia - "in that it had no majority ethnic population." A major consequence of this fact for someone trying to re-establish the Croatian Banovina, such as the accused in this case, and bring Bosnia's Croats into Croatia was that this not only involved redrawing lines on the map, but moving populations, moving large populations, sometimes your population, your own population, and sometimes somebody else's population. One instance which illustrates this was a meeting on the 8th of January, 1992, during which Tudjman, Susak, a Bosnian Croat leader named Franjo Boras, a Bosnian Serb leader named Nikola Koljevic, met together with no Muslims present and discussed Bosnia's partition and a resettlement of the populations. And the Serb Koljevic described in that meeting -- he talked about Bosnia's ethnic population again being a leopard skin and said that the three ethnic groups, Croats, Serbs, and Muslims, should have the opportunity for "normal development" with the nations living "next to each other but not on top of each other." Koljevic went on to say: "Yes, the homogeneity of certain areas. We even thought about it because we noticed that people are already simply moving, they are exchanging flats on their own, that it would be a good idea to establish an agency which would regulate the exchange of property and raise this to a civilised level ... It is not so impossible to divide Bosnia. You know, everything is possible ... Look at that leopard's skin ..." To which Tudjman replied: "... such a principled agreement means that we should be forthcoming with respect to territorial delimitation, and that is acceptable because in this regard history shows that not only was such understanding necessary, but also population exchanges, and so forth." "Wherever national problems so conceived emerged as they did with us, that was resolved, from World War I and World War II, that was brought to a conclusion by exchanges ..." Exchanges of population. Indeed, only a few days earlier, Tudjman had talked about a map redrawing the ethnic areas. "Why not accept an offer of demarcation when it is in the interest of the Croatian people ... because I do not see a single reason, a serious reason against it. ... one of our people in Bosnia drafted a proposal for demarcation whereby the Croatian areas and those that you have included in this Community of Herceg-Bosna and the Community of the Croatian Posavina ... in the event of demarcation, Croatia would not only -- would get not only those two communities, but also, for geopolitical reasons, Cazinska and Bihacka Krajina which would satisfy almost ideally the Croatian national interest, not only present but also for the future ... And to create a statelet, therefore, out of the remaining part around Sarajevo where mostly Muslims and some Catholic Croats would stay which would resemble the small historical land of Bosnia. It would, therefore, be a buffer zone in the demarcation of Serbia and Croatia and in such conditions it would have to rely on Croatia to a large extent." Now, with all that in mind, if you look at map 8 which is now displayed, this once again shows the municipalities of Bosnia and Herzegovina with the borders of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and will not feature prominently in this case but at the same time, in parallel fashion as the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was created, the Croatian Community of Bosanski Posavina in the northern corner of Bosnia-Herzegovina was created using the same methods and again following closely the borders of the banovina of 1939 as they encroached into that part of Bosnia. But focusing our attention now on Herceg-Bosna, you will see -- and you can see the legend. The areas that are in a solid light blue are those areas with a Croatian majority. That is more than 50 per cent of the population was Croat. Then you see areas which you might say are hatched with blue and this buff or yellow colour, and those are the areas that there was a relative Croat majority. They didn't have a majority but they had what some would call a plurality, more than the next large percentage group. Now, what you see, what this map makes clear, is that within the borders claimed by Herceg-Bosna, there were indeed probably almost half but certainly many municipalities and areas that were not Croat areas at all. They were not Croat majority areas. They were not Croat plurality areas. In fact, they were areas in which Muslims had a plurality or majority. If you go to the next map. Again, you just see the borders. But if this is what you want, if this is your goal, to carve out and create the Herceg-Bosna as it's defined here, all blue, but what you really have is this. You see, if you will, "the problem." You want it all. You want all the areas in blue but you don't have it all, and you have this problem with Muslims who, in fact, live in these areas that are not either light blue or hatched in the way that they are. Therein, if you will, lies the problem. It was in this situation that Mate Boban became the president of Herceg-Bosna, stated a key component of the Greater Croatia Herceg-Bosna plan that would be carried out with so much violence and so much destruction over the next two or three years. Boban: "The founding municipalities of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, the HZ HB, now have a population which according to the census is 55 per cent Croatian, 27 per cent Muslim, 9 per cent Serbia and the rest are none of the above. However, because municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina were created, similarly as in Croatia, by composing Serbian and Muslim populations in the territory of Croatia or vice versa, by cleansing the border areas, practically the border areas of Herceg-Bosna, this creates approximately 65 per cent of the Croatian population in Herceg-Bosna." In fact, even as early as June of 1991, Tudjman had indicated that inevitably the Muslim leadership would have to accept Bosnia's division. "I think we shall achieve it because this is equally in the interests of Serbia and Croatia, while the Muslim component has no other exit than to accept this solution, although it will not be easy to find the solution, but, essentially, that is it." Now, another component of what this -- what the evidence will show is that as to the areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina most related to this case, there was in fact very little disagreement between the Croats and Serbs on their basic territorial claims. And we will come back to that later in the opening statement, but I will show you one map now. This is a map of the claims made, territorial claims or borders claimed by the Bosnian Serb autonomous areas as of January 1992. And the Serbs at that time are claiming these five different, if you will, districts or autonomous areas, SAOs, in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And when you look at that map, and there again you have the borders in bright blue of so-called Herceg-Bosna, you will note that by and large there is very little overlap or conflict between the Croat claims and the Serb claims with the exception of a few -- the municipality of Kupres up toward the -- roughly to the left of the middle of the map, up north and Kotor Varos, and down south there was a little bit of overlap in the area of Trebinje. But by and large, there was no great dispute. The Croats had their claims on Bosnia, and the Serbs had their claims on Bosnia. In early May of 1992, the Bosnian Croat leader Mate Boban, and Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic held secret meetings at Graz, Austria, to confirm agreement on the Croats' and Serbs' territorial claims. A press release was issued as a result of this meeting which set out the broad areas of agreement and reserved several areas of disagreement. In the public statement that was issued on the 6th of May, 1992: "In the city of Mostar, the Serbian side considers the Neretva River -" which runs through the city of Mostar - "to be the borderline, while the Croatian side considers the entire city of Mostar to be within the Croatian constituent unit." "South of Mostar the Croatian side considers the entire area delineated in 1939, in other words, the borders of the Hrvatska Banovina, to be within the Croatian constituent unit. The Serbian side considers the Neretva River to be the borderline between the Croatian and Serbian constituent units." Now, these statements and statements like it around this time in 1992 on the carve-up of the state of Bosnia by Serbs and Croats begged the obvious question: "Where do these borders leave the Muslims?" If the Serbs have everything on one side of the Neretva and the Croats have everything on the other side of the Neretva, then where was the kind of dark humour, the dark answer, the question that was circulated around that time among the Muslims in Herzegovina and the answer was: In the Neretva. That is, the Muslims would be in the river. In September of 1992, Tudjman reminded Susak and the accused Slobodan Praljak that the banovina was already part of Croatia and not to go beyond the banovina. In considering Tudjman's statement, let's look again at this map, showing the overlay of the banovina extending well into Bosnia and Herzegovina. Tudjman to Praljak and Susak on the 11th of September: "Gentlemen, gentlemen ... we have nothing to conquer, let's defend those Croatian ..." Praljak: "Nowhere, Mr. President, it is impossible to pass further." Tudjman: "And let's get ready to cleanse them out of Croatia. As I said, -- do not get involved in conquering Bosnia." Praljak: "No, Mr. President, believe me, the attacks have stopped. Susak: "Nothing out of the banovina, we did not trespass, not even one metre. Tudjman: "Don't, because -- listen, we have, let's be realistic, we have hardly escaped, both, the Islamic government and the world, to have sanctions imposed on us -- because we are, allegedly, also aggressors in Bosnia, those who are conquering Bosnia. Accordingly, don't do it. Susak: "President, here we were disciplined to the maximum." Tudjman's territorial ambitions did not go away even after the Washington Agreement that resolved at least the large-scale open fighting between the Croats and Muslims. And in May of 1994, Tudjman told Herceg-Bosna leaders, including one of our accused, Mr. Prlic, and Dario Kordic, the convicted war criminal, convicted at this ICTY, and others: " ... we must pursue our policy in such a way as to take control of Bosnia without imposing [ourselves] in a way which would provoke the Muslims and drive them to revolt, see? We will conduct a smart policy. We have to be seen as siding with the Muslims, but we don't want them to create their Muslim state and that poses a problem." Tudjman told the Herceg-Bosna leaders to get the Muslims to declare themselves "Croats of Muslim faith ..." "Get down to it right now, we have no other choice." As I have made reference to already, the events leading to the establishment and operation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- Herzegovina began not in Bosnia but in Croatia, in a series of meetings in Zagreb. By 1990 and 1991, Tudjman and his party, the HDZ, had established and organised a branch of that same party in Bosnia called the HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Tudjman and the Zagreb party controlled the Bosnian branch of the party. High-ranking HDZ officials and members from Zagreb were almost always in attendance at HDZ meetings in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Again, a number these meetings have been established by Tribunal judgements. A meeting on the 26th of August, 1991, steps being taken to link the HDZ Municipal Boards together, adjudicated fact number 47, a meeting again about linking the municipalities with majority Croat populations and of a "special plan." Adjudicated fact number 48, referring to a meeting involving several of the leaders and the establishment of the regional communities, including the Travnik regional community in Central Bosnia. In a further record of one of these meetings, the August -- the August 1991 meeting, which it was stated in the records of that meeting which was called a proposal for the regionalisation of the municipal committees of the Croatian Democratic Union: "In keeping with these conclusions -- the conclusions passed by the Bosnia-Herzegovina HDZ Main Board on the 6th of August, we propose a regionalisation of the BH HDZ Municipal Boards. The purpose of this regionalisation is to create the best possible links between the BH HDZ Municipal Boards on a territorial principle which is a prerequisite for the creation of the political and territorial linking of the Croatian people, for which purpose special programmes will have to be drawn up." The next step toward creating Herceg-Bosna was to then combine these regional communities into one single entity. Tudjman himself set out this process in a meeting on the 12th of November, 1991. Tudjman: "The Croatian people in general expect the directions from us on what to do ... We have been holding back until now. We said, 'Wait, we cannot question, we cannot endanger the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina because of the defence of the Republic of Croatia borders' ... but it seems to me that we have reached a phase when certain steps should be made ... "Therefore, I believe if that they want us, they want me to state my opinion immediately. A certain delegation should come to visit me and I think that at this moment that we should tell them, to say that they exist as a the regional community of Croatian municipalities." Now, that is on the 12th of November, 1991. It cannot have a been a coincidence, Mr. President and Your Honours, it cannot have been a coincidence that on this very same day, the 12th of November, 1991, at an HDZ party leadership meeting called by the Herzegovina and Travnik regional communities headed by Mate Boban and Dario Kordic respectively, the stage was set for the actual decision a few days later, to in fact establish the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. You will see on the slide that is before you now which comes from Exhibit 71, P71 part of the records of that meeting. Directing your attention to those parts that are emphasised: "We must finally carry out a decisive and active policy which should lead to the realisation of our centuries-old dream - a joint Croatian state." And at the end: " ... and the creation of a sovereign Croatia in its ethnic and historical (now possible) borders." Then only a few days later on the 18th of November, 1991, six days later, the HDZ party, or at least the more nationalist elements of that party, including again Boban, Kordic and others, declared the existence of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna as a separate "political, cultural, economic, and territorial whole." Stating in its decision the declaration establishing the so-called Herceg-Bosna, being deeply aware that their future lies with the future of the entire Croatian people, referring to the right of people to self-determination and sovereignty, and rejecting -- or that is indicating the unacceptability of the unitary state model, that based on these things the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is hereby established. In that same document there is a listing of the municipalities included. I'm not going to read them all to you now, but they're on the map and they will be shown in the documents and evidence that you will have. But again we now have here the borders of what was declared in November 1991 as the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And once again you put on the banovina overlay. There's Herceg-Bosna. There's the banovina. No coincidence, Your Honours. No coincidence that the borders of the Herceg-Bosna were almost identical to the borders of the banovina of 1939. The establishment of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna and its intention to succeed from Bosnia and Herzegovina are again established by adjudicated facts at this Tribunal. Adjudicated fact number 58. "The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna consisted of 30 municipalities (including those in Central Bosnia) and was described as a 'political, economic and territorial integrity.'" And adjudicated fact number 59: "... the HZ HB was founded with the intention that it should secede from Bosnia and Herzegovina and with a view to unification with Croatia." The substance of the earlier pleadings going back to at least June 1991, the meetings in Zagreb, was summarised by the leader Dario Kordic at the 27 December meeting with Tudjman and others. Kordic told Tudjman: "For six months we have been sweating blood, deliberating over the idea that you presented to us on the 13th and 20th of June. For six months we've been dealing with this." Kordic made it clear that he was discussing the partition of Bosnia: "I think that any other option would be considered treason, save the clear demarcation of Croatian soil in the territory of Herceg-Bosna ..." Going further in that same meeting to the next slide. I just mention briefly, in the interests of time, that as part of -- again, the records, the minutes of the meeting that was held on the 23rd of December, a few days before the December meeting, talking about the creation of Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna "... which serves as a legal basis for the entry of these territories into the Republic of Croatia." And further, rejecting -- you can see toward the end of the slide, rejecting -- "The legitimacy of Alija Izetbegovic, the president of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to represent the Croatian people ... is hereby revoked ..." We want to be part of Croatia. We reject the Bosnian government. We reject the leadership. We are no part of it. Tudjman gave his full support to the Herceg-Bosna strategy as indeed it was largely his plan or a plan that he and others had developed and then implemented. It was at this same 27 December meeting that I mentioned earlier where Tudjman indicated that the banovina borders could be accomplished with the Muslims being left with a small statelet around Sarajevo and where Boban made the statements how Herceg-Bosna could be further strengthened or accomplished by cleansing the border areas. I'll make a short reference to the referendum on Bosnia and Herzegovina independence in February of 1992. There was indeed a referendum in February of that year to determine whether Bosnia and Herzegovina should be declared independent of the former Yugoslavia, which had this question on the ballot: "Are you for a sovereign and independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, a state of citizens and peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina with equal rights, Muslims, Serbs, Croats, and members of other peoples who live in it?" While most Bosnian Serbs boycotted the referendum and Bosnian Croat voting on the first day of the referendum of the two days of voting was light, ultimately Bosnian Croat appears -- Bosnian Croat population largely supported the referendum and voted yes, and in fact the referendum passed. Now, there is sometimes a reference to this as establishing -- as being somehow an indication that indeed the Croats supported Bosnia-Herzegovina. Your Honours, as you consider the facts and the evidence in the case, consider the alternative. The alternative of not voting for independence was to remain in Milosevic's Yugoslavia, and at least getting -- taking it one step at a time, better to establish the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a step toward Greater Croatia than to remain in Milosevic's Yugoslavia. Thereafter that, Your Honours, began series of steps that were taken to put fully into place the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and to establish what became known as the Croatian Defence Council, or the HVO. That was declared on the 8th of April, 1992. It was declared as Herceg-Bosna's supreme defence body. Note the language of the declaration. "To defend the sovereignty of the territories." It did not say to defend parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It did not say to defend a club or association or grouping of people. It said "the sovereignty of the territories." Giving a full indication of the intent behind this declaration and the goals and objectives of the Croatian Defence Council, or HVO. Two days later, on the 10th of April, 1992, the Herceg-Bosna authorities went even further. Not only was the HVO the supreme defence body, it was the only legal armed force on the territories claimed by Herceg-Bosna, and all others, including the armed forces of the internationally recognised sovereign state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is the government forces, were illegal and enemy formations. They are the enemy, and we do not recognise them. Further, on the 15th of May, 1992, the Croatian Defence Council, it said, "shall be established as the supreme executive and administrative body in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." In effect what you had, Your Honours, what the evidence will show is the Croatian Defence Council, the HVO, which combined political, administrative, executive and military power. You had an executive form of government, which the evidence will show how it operated, effectively combining and putting the hands of power -- or putting power into the hands of a few select people, including many of the accused in this case. In the course of the evidence, as you've heard already this afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, you will hear the reference to Herceg-Bosna or to the HVO. Typically, the entity, if you will, the country or the so-called state, was referred to as Herceg-Bosna, whereas the structures or the government or the military was commonly referred to as the Croatian Defence Council, or HVO. From the very beginning Herceg-Bosna acted as a state and the HVO acted as a government, complete with laws, armed forces, police, customs and taxes in direct opposition to the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Even by the 17th of September, 1992, less than year after the declaration in November of 1991, Jadranko Prlic reported to Tudjman: "We have organised the authorities. This is only starting. We have an Official Gazette. We are passing the necessary decrees, and we are trying to take care of -- to take care of that aspect in the liberated territories." Now, as the evidence will show that, as a further consolidation of governmental or administrative power, military power, in August of 1993, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was then declared to be not the Community but the Republic of Herceg-Bosna on the 28th of August, 1993. In most respects not a substantial change for our purposes or for purposes of the case. Most of the governmental processes remained largely the same but again even a further indication to claims of statehood, being the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. The evidence will show that in fact Tudjman and his fellow travellers in Zagreb controlled the Herceg-Bosna government just as much as they controlled the political part of the HDZ. On the 30th of September of 1993, Susak himself indicated "that Zagreb controlled Mate Boban even when it came to the selection of a Prime Minister and members of a government ..." "Susak: Boban has not composed the government yet, and I have told him to nominate the Premier today, so the parliament can adopt him and then the Premier can nominate the government. Today, he will designate Prlic before the parliament for the adoption."

utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to have a break so that Mr. Prlic can also have a rest. It is 3.30. We shall resume at ten to four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing has resumed. Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In discussing again the creation of the Herceg-Bosna state and its advancement as such, we would also refer to a statement by Mr. Prlic on the 13th of February, 1994. "... we have created a state in Herceg-Bosna with all systems, including customs and finance. People are born and die with Herceg-Bosna documents. I think we should weigh all the elements carefully. Absolutely no solution is acceptable without a Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, in other words, a Croatian Republic, and the borders should encompass as many areas as possible in the whole of Central Bosnia. I believe we can achieve this, by military means if necessary, in order to make sure that things are developing the way they are developing ..." And indeed by even much earlier than February 1994, by the latter part of 1992, Herceg-Bosna was acting, for all intents and purposes, as an extension of Croatia on Bosnia's territory. In May 1993, a high-level report by the European Community Monitoring Mission stated, in fact what I just said, to all intents and purposes, much of Herceg-Bosna was by late 1992 behaving as an integral part of Croatia. It might be noted here before continuing on, Mr. President, that neither the sovereign state of Bosnia and Herzegovina nor the international community itself ever recognised Herceg-Bosna as a legal state or legal entity. In fact, the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina declared both the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and later the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna illegal on or about the 14th of September, 1992, and the 20th of January, 1994, respectively. Following Herceg-Bosna's establishment in November 1991, and especially from May 1992 forward, the Herceg-Bosna HVO leadership, including the accused and other leaders and members of the joint criminal enterprise, engaged in continuing and coordinated efforts to dominate and, if you will, Croatise the municipalities which they claimed as part of Herceg-Bosna with increasing persecution and discrimination directed against the Bosnian Muslim population. The HVO took control of many municipal governments and services, removing or marginalising Muslim leaders. They took control of the media, and they imposed Croatian ideas and propaganda. Croatian symbols and currency were introduced, Croatian curricula in the schools, and "the so-called Croatian language" was introduced in schools. Many Bosnian Muslims were removed from positions in government and private business. Humanitarian aid was managed and manipulated in such a way to the Muslims' disadvantage, and Muslims in general were increasingly harassed. As I indicated earlier, the Herceg-Bosna leadership declared Mostar as Herceg-Bosna's capital and set about making or attempting to make Mostar into a Croat city, despite the fact, despite the important fact that Croats comprised only a little over a third of its population in the city of Mostar itself as its second largest ethnic group. While the defence of Mostar against the Serbs was initially contemplated as a joint Croat-Muslim effort and indeed a 29 April 1992 agreement providing for the HVO to lead the town's military defence based on Joint Command structure existed, it was by no means permission or approval for the HVO seizing all power, including all government, military, and political power. The HVO, however, quickly asserted overall control, and most of the multi-ethnic command staff was either removed or marginalised. If I could have the assistance of the technical booth, please, in showing the next clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "Croats mount an all-out assault in Mostar. The Bosnian forces resist. "Have you always seen Mostar as the capital of Herceg-Bosna? "Yes, all the time. "Even though it was a majority Muslim ... "No, there are no majority in Mostar, of any nation. Before the war, the equal number of inhabitants were Muslims and Croats. Difference was only few hundred. "But still you saw it as the capital of the Croatian part of Bosnia-Herzegovina? "Yes. "Why? "Yes, it is. Because this republic must have a capital, must have one centre, must have university, must have other things which makes republic a republic on one civilisation level, the theatre, the symphonic orchestra and so on."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The self-declared Herceg-Bosna HVO institutions demanded and seized power in one municipality after another. And you will see documents ultimately showing the assertion of HVO control over one municipality after another, almost like a series of dominoes coming under the control of the HVO. But not only that, but the HVO systematic taking of power largely followed a set pattern, a recognisable pattern. There was often an initial pretext that shared multi-ethnic bodies under joint control or command where possible in resisting the so-called Serb aggressor, but in a short time most previously elected officials, duly elected officials, in multi-ethnic institutions were replaced by HVO appointed officials. Indeed, early on the Herceg-Bosna HVO leadership contemplated and foresaw from the beginning that most Bosnian Muslims would resist Herceg-Bosna being imposed on them. Again, at the important 27 December 1991 meeting in Zagreb, Boban said, "I think that the Muslim people are practically -- I'm not defending them, when it comes to my personal opinion, I would also want Croatia, the one in the borders of 50-60 years ago -" the banovina - "but I think that it is hard to divide them. They are a people with their own firm positions and I think it will be very hard. As soon as Herceg-Bosna emerged there were objections from Jablanica, for instance, and from other places, which are not accepting such conceptions." In fact, and as Boban predicted, and as the others must have plainly foreseen, most Bosnian Muslims did not accept HVO control even when it was thrust upon them against their will. It was patently clear that Tudjman's and the Herceg-Bosna leadership's Greater Croatia could not be achieved by only political or peaceful means. Instead, clearly necessary components and plainly foreseeable results and aspects of the enterprise were political and religious persecution, ethnic violence, armed conflict, and forcible -- forcible involuntary population transfers. In short, what unfortunately became known in the 1990s as "ethnic cleansing." Once it became apparent that the Muslims would not go quietly into that good night which was the partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Tudjman and his Herceg-Bosna collaborators formulated and carried out a policy to take the territories by force and population displacement. The establishment and implementation of this programme plainly demonstrates the existence and workings of the joint criminal enterprise, the existence of an international armed conflict involving the Republic of Croatia on the sovereign territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the widespread and systematic nature of the persecutions, attacks, and other conduct directed against the Bosnian Muslim population. Some forms of persecution were a simple or subtle, or perhaps not so subtle, as the use of symbols, flags, songs, and similar devices. All of this know, Mr. President and Your Honours, that symbols can have a powerful effect on people. They can be powerful forces for good or they can be powerful forces for evil or for bad. Symbols can play a very, very telling role in a culture and in a society, and in this instance Herceg-Bosna was no different. The Herceg-Bosna leadership right away went on to impose and create their own symbols and flags and insignia to make sure it was very clear that this was Croatian territory. We'll show you a couple of slides. What you see now on the screen is the flag of the Republic of Croatia itself, the State of Croatia. Go to the next. This is the -- just a part of the flag, essentially part of the flag, the coat of arms, and you'll see some icons on top of the chequerboard. Now you can see the Herceg-Bosna or HVO flag. Identical, virtually identical, except that instead of having the icons that we saw earlier on top of the chequerboard portion, we have these symbols that you see here. Likewise in terms of military insignia, here you have a patch of the Croatian army, the HV, the army of the Republic of Croatia, and the next slide you have the patch of the HVO. Not only were these -- were symbols and flags and such things used but Croatian money, the dinar, was introduced and clearly encouraged or required by the Herceg-Bosna HVO authorities even though the dinar, the Croatian dinar, was an extremely weak currency at the time. One of the first areas in which the HVO demonstrated its early intention to create a purely Croat space in Herceg-Bosna was education. They renamed the Mostar university, which had been multi-ethnic and had been named after Dzemal Bijedic to the Croat -- instead to the Croat University in Mostar. The university board was stacked with Croat members along with a small number of hand-picked acceptable Muslims. The Croatian -- "Croatian language" was introduced in schools. As early as June of 1992, the HVO commander and accused Milivoj Petkovic reported to the municipal leadership and commanders of the HVO units: "Today we have under control almost the entire territory of the Croatian municipalities (Neum, Ravno, Stolac, Capljina, Ljubuski, Citluk, Siroki Brijeg and Mostar). Admittedly, there are still part of the territory, mostly in Mostar and Stolac municipalities, that are not under control of HVO forces. Therefore, we have four main tasks in front of us: One, to put under control the remaining area of Croatian municipalities; two, to secure and fortify the achieved line; three, to carry out the reorganisation of the existing HVO forces; and four, to establish Croatian rule over all municipalities." Now, a basic blueprint, virtually an HVO blueprint for taking over municipal governments and power can be seen in the minutes of a 22nd of September, 1992, meeting in which various municipalities give virtually a progress report on the HVO takeover municipality by municipality. You'll see just some excerpts from this record, the minutes of a meeting where various municipalities give a report. "Novi Travnik: It is estimated the HVO holds about 70 per cent of the power ... The HVO is charging 50 per cent retail tax immediately when using trading permits. State tax -- in Fojnica state tax is collected by the HVO. Schools have not started operating in the Croatian language. Bugojno: The Croatian dinar is accepted means of payment. Kiseljak: The HVO is in complete control. Television centre is under construction in Kiseljak. Elementary and secondary schools have started working in the Croatian language." Et cetera, et cetera. Takeover of one municipality after another by the HVO and the imposition of Croat culture and ideas and symbols on the Muslim population. Indeed, by September 1994, Mr. Prlic told the president -- told President Tudjman: "Mr. President, every Croat in Bosnia and Herzegovina is a paid Croat. Everyone is on the salary of the Herceg-Bosna budget except for the part that is in Serbian territory." Now, on the question of Serbian territory, I'm going to begin to abbreviate some of the topics that I had hoped to discuss in the opening statement, but I'll just cover it a bit more quickly. But as I said earlier, in fact the evidence will show -- and this will be important, Your Honours, and the reason I'm taking the time to address it is because I believe it will be important as you hear the evidence from both sides. The evidence will show that for the most part, again, there was no fundamental conflict between the Croats and Serbs in 1992 and 1993 in the areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina most relevant to this case. I'm not talking about other parts of Bosnia. I'm not talking about Eastern Bosnia, around Tuzla or those portions, I'm talking about the portions of the Mostar region in Herzegovina. Now, again let me be clear: I'm not saying -- the Prosecution does not -- does not contend that there were not some local skirmishes between Serb and Croat units, and indeed, unfortunately, I'm sure persons on both sides lost their lives in some conflict, but that was not the fundamental situation. Instead, and much more substantially, this was a time of extensive Croat and Serb cooperation and indeed collusion to the disadvantage of the Muslims. In fact, the Croats and Serbs continued to accommodate -- accommodate each other's principal territorial needs, with Tudjman recognising, for example, that the Serbs had a reasonable need for a corridor through the Posavina in north-east Bosnia-Herzegovina, that it was part of the Serbs' basic conditions and it was of vital importance to them and it should be allowed. Now, note that. Tudjman saying it should be allowed. Well, who was Tudjman to say what should be allowed, a territory belonging to the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina? But according to Tudjman, it was okay for the Serbs to make those claims. In a similar fashion, Slobodan Milosevic supported the Croats' demands in late 1993 to have a corridor through Gornji Vakuf to link the claimed Croat territories in Herzegovina and Central Bosnia. Tudjman also claimed that the Serbs had recognised Kupres as Croat territory, and the Croats would have to give the Serbs something in return. The Croats and Serbs carving up Bosnia and Herzegovina, each for their own interest. Indeed, when under international pressure, the possibility of peace with the Bosnian Muslims was considered by Tudjman and his advisors in late September 1993. Serious concerns were expressed on how this changed relationship with the Muslims would affect the Croats' good cooperation with the Serbs. Mr. Praljak, as a party to this conversation, expressed his great concern, saying, "The relations between the Croats and the Serbs have improved, especially on the military plain, because our whole units depend on cooperation with the Serbs. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, this agreement," that is the agreement with the Muslims, "will aggravate that a lot. Therefore, Zepca, Kiseljak, and thus Vitez, the battalion below Konjic and Vares, it will now be difficult for us to provide them with supplies. "Tudjman: But fighting against the Muslims should stop. "Praljak: It will stop, but this is going to be different. A year ago we thought we could not hold talks with the Serbs at all. We have reached some agreement with the Serbs, and now we should start a war against them in order to ease the tensions with the Muslims. It will probably take time to turn things around psychologically." Indeed, by the 220th of December 1993 the UN itself had recognised the collusion. I direct your attention in the interests of time to the highlighted language of this UN General Assembly document referring to the "Collusion between Serbian forces and extremist Bosnian Croat elements and others to seek the dismemberment of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina ..." This takes us then forward to the first major clash, the first major armed clash between the Croats and Muslims in October of 1992 in Prozor and Novi Travnik as charged in the indictment. Despite some cooperation in the spring and summer of 1992, you will probably understand, I hope, in fact in connection with what I have said so far this afternoon that tensions and conflicts between the Herceg-Bosna HVO structures and the Bosnian Muslims continued and increased or, putting it a different way, their relationship deteriorated over time. By mid-September 1992, the Croats were preparing for a war with the Muslims. In fact, on the 11th of September, Praljak said: "War with the Muslims can be anticipated." And Susak answered: "We have been aware of that for over a week now and we have made preparations on what needs to be done." And it was only about approximately a month or five weeks later after Susak says, we've already known about that, we've already put the preparations in place, but the fighting and conflict broke out in the Prozor-Novi Travnik area around the 19th of October, 1992. If we can look at the next slide. Again, you'll find Prozor, if you look -- if you see the Herceg-Bosna blue area, approximately the middle of that you will see the municipality of Prozor, to give you some orientation. With Jablanica immediately to the south and Gornji Vakuf to the north. If you go on, please. This will show a -- it's the overall map and diagram of Prozor municipality and some of the principal towns and locations in Prozor. And the red stars -- the red stars being areas where crimes occurred according to the indictment and according to the case that the evidence will show where various crimes charged in the indictment occurred. Next you will see again a map showing the ethnic or demographic characteristics of Prozor based on the 1991 census. Largely a mixture, as you will see, of the red Croat areas and green Muslim areas. On the morning of the 23rd of October, 1992, the HVO president in Prozor told the Bosnian Muslims that the increasing Croat-Muslim tensions would be solved by the Muslims immediately accepting Herceg-Bosna HVO political and military control. "You want peace? You want to avoid conflict? Then just give in to our demands. Accept our power. Accept our control, and you won't have any problems." Unfortunately, the Muslims declined to go voluntarily. Later that day on the 23rd of October, in the afternoon, Herceg-Bosna HVO forces attacked the Muslims in Prozor town. On the 23rd and 24th of October, 1992, after they had taken control of Prozor, the Herceg-Bosna HVO forces plundered, burned, and destroyed Bosnian Muslim homes and other properties. On the 24th of October, the HVO forces rounded up Muslims in the area promising that no harm would come to them. In fact, the HVO forces arrested the Bosnian Muslim men and detained them in the Ripci primary school. Some of the Muslim men were kept for several days while others were kept for several weeks. HVO forces severely beat a number of the Muslim detainees. Also on the 24th of October, HVO forces attacked a nearby Muslim village of Paljike, one kilometre south of Prozor town. They deliberately destroyed Bosnian Muslim homes and property killing a number of Muslim civilians. By the evening of the 24th of October, the HVO reported that Prozor town was "ethnically pure," the Muslim population having either been detained or fled. You'll see part of that report in the slide that was there. "The two areas are ethnically pure. The Muslim population has been detained or has fled." On October the 26th of 1992, Bruno Stojic, Milivoj Petkovic, Janko Bobetko and others were informed the HVO had taken control of Prozor on the 25th of October with many casualties on the Muslim side. The HVO now controls the entire area around lake Rama, the town of Prozor, the dam at the lake, the hydroelectric power plant and the road to Jablanica up until the Jasna settlement. As a precursor of things to come and as already repeatedly demonstrated in the armed conflict and ethnic violence in the former Yugoslavia that had already occurred by October 1992, the HVO actions in Prozor in October involved the widespread burning of Muslim houses and a number of killings. Slobodan Praljak, who was then also Croatia's assistant minister of defence, joined the HVO celebrations in Prozor and said that the conflict "didn't bode well for the Bosniaks in Herzegovina." That is, the Muslims. Now, we're proceeding, Mr. President, roughly chronologically. Around this time, by the fall of 1992, late 1992, there were various international peace efforts to stop the fighting and the violence and conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and around this time and by early January 1993 what was being discussed was the so-called Vance-Owen Peace Plan. In January, United Nations and European Community peace negotiators met in Geneva with Croat, Serb, and Muslim representatives and discussed a proposed peace agreement. While neither the Serbs nor Muslims had agreed to the Vance-Owen proposals, by mid-January 1993 Franjo Tudjman, Gojko Susak and the Herceg-Bosna HVO leadership found the plan as they envisioned and interpreted it much to their favour essentially giving them the Croatian Banovina and even additional territory covered by the proposed Vance-Owen provinces, 3, 8, and 10, despite the fact, once again, that many of these areas included provinces that had a majority or at least equal Muslim populations and were controlled or occupied by the Bosnian government armed forces. Indeed, the Vance-Owen proposal appeared to give the Croats, who comprised at that time approximately not in one particular area but overall approximately 17.5 per cent of the Bosnia-Herzegovina population, approximately 28 per cent of the overall territory. Once again, in a map configuration which substantially corresponded to the banovina or even more. And you'll see on the display now a -- the proposed Vance-Owen Peace Plan map, at least as it existed as of January of 1993, and the assignment or proposed assignment of various provinces to various principal ethnic groups. And you will see that the province, proposed provinces 10 and 8 in Herzegovina being proposed as Croat areas, and you'll see that that again roughly very closely corresponds to both Herceg-Bosna and to the territory claimed by the banovina on the maps that we saw earlier. And in fact Tudjman himself confirmed that the territorial provision of the Vance-Owen Plan roughly accomplished the banovina. Tudjman said in June 1993: "This is roughly what in 1939," that is the provinces 3, 8, and 10, "this is roughly what in 1939 became part of the banovina of Croatia." There is no mistake about that. In mid-January of 1993, the Herceg-Bosna HVO leadership was so eager to implement their vision of this very favourable plan in their view and as interpreted by them that they refused to wait for the Muslims and Serbs to accept it and instead took unilateral action to implement it on their own. This, even though the Vance-Owen talks at that particular time in Geneva were that and only that, talks. No agreement, no signed plan, simply talks. And in fact and in looking ahead, the Vance-Owen Plan was never agreed or never implemented. Unfortunately later in 1993, it died for lack of agreement. The Serbs never did agree to it, and there were always continuing conflicts about it. At a meeting in Zagreb on the 15th of January, 1993, Tudjman, Susak, and Boban failed to convince Izetbegovic to accept their views. 15th of January, Izetbegovic says: "The Herceg-Bosna HVO authorities had disenfranchised the Muslims of Mostar, who comprised half of the city's population, and that the authorities had elsewhere dissolved legal governments whose members had been freely elected." Further in that paragraph, Izetbegovic says: "That's not how I understood the papers, and I don't know whether this was the intention of those documents. Because I do not see that they define who has what territories, whose armies these are, you know. So I'm afraid that what is now going on in Gornji Vakuf may have been caused by a misunderstanding of this item of these agreements ... it was not foreseen that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina should leave either the Travnik province or Mostar. That's not how I understand these papers." Now, Mr. President, please note that date, 15th of January, 1993, and on that date President Izetbegovic had made it very clear to the assembled Croat and Bosnian-Croat leadership that he did not accept or endorse their views. He did not agree these were Croat territories. It was very clear. Despite that, despite knowing that, on that very same day, the 15th of January, 1993, the HVO President Jadranko Prlic signed a decision that: "All units of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which at this moment are stationed in provinces 3, 8, and 10, which have been declared Croatian provinces under the Geneva Accords -" accords that didn't exist yet - "shall be subordinated to the command of the Main Staff of the HVO armed forces. The deadline for implementing this decision is hereby set at five days starting from today, 15th of January, 1993." Now, look at the sequence of events. On the 15th of January Izetbegovic is meeting in Zagreb with Tudjman, Boban, and others, and says, "Your views are not acceptable. I do not agree to them." On the very same day, the 15th of January, Jadranko Prlic issues a decision, an ultimatum, saying, "If you don't subordinate Muslim forces to us within five --" You have five days to do so, essentially, or leave the municipalities. The Prlic decision was then followed -- handed down the HVO chain of command, with the Defence Minister Bruno Stojic issuing a similar order, the minister of defence. Again you can read the language there for yourself. "Members of the units who do not leave the territory of the province and do not wish to subordinate themselves to the relevant command shall be treated as members of paramilitary units who shall be disarmed and taken into custody." The deadline the 20th of January, 1993. And from the minister of defence, the order then went down to the head of the army, the senior military commander, Milivoj Petkovic, who again on the same day, 15th of January, 1993, issued an order implementing the order -- the decision of Jadranko Prlic and implementing the orders of his immediate superior, Bruno Stojic, the minister of defence. As the 20th of January deadline approached and passed, the first major armed conflict between the HVO and the Muslims since Prozor in October 1992 broke out in several parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, including at Gornji Vakuf and Busovaca. Which brings us to the next set of crimes charged in the indictment, the crimes occurring in Gornji Vakuf in January of 1993. Now, here again to orient the Chamber, you will see on the map up in the -- toward the top -- top middle portion of the blue area of Herceg-Bosna, you will see the municipality of Gornji Vakuf, then with Prozor to the south and Novi Travnik to the north. And again you'll see a map of the Gornji Vakuf municipality. And the red stars being areas of alleged crimes. And also a demographic map of the municipality showing the demographic composition of the municipality as it existed in the 1991 census. What we've seen, then, is by the 15th of January, 1993, Prlic, Stojic, and Petkovic had all issued their decisions and orders directing that the Bosnian army, or ABiH forces, the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in large parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, including Gornji Vakuf, either subordinate themselves to the HVO or withdraw from these areas. In addition to this general ultimatum, on the 16th of January the following day, the HVO issued a specific ultimatum to the Muslims in Gornji Vakuf demanding that they withdraw from the area by midnight on the 17th of January. Again, the Muslims rejected the HVO ultimatum. Slobodan Praljak, commanding the HVO forces at the time, then sent a message to the ABiH that they would be "annihilated if they do not accept the decisions of the HZ HB." By the 18th of January, 1993, following the expiration of the deadline at midnight on the 17th, HVO forces, true to the ultimatum, immediately attacked the Bosnian Muslims in Gornji Vakuf. In Gornji Vakuf town and in several surrounding villages, including Duse, Hrasnica, Uzricja, and Zdrimci. HVO attacks and artillery killed a number of Muslim civilians and destroyed or damaged a substantial amount of Muslim property, which is further set out in the indictment and in the annex to the indictment. Following the HVO attack on Duse and these other villages, the HVO plundered and burned Bosnian Muslim houses and property in and around these villages. The HVO robbed hundreds of arrested or captured Bosnian Muslims, separated the Muslim men from the Muslim women, children, and elderly. In most instances, the Herceg-Bosna HVO forces took the Muslim men away to HVO detention facilities while they detained the women, children, and elderly in one or two houses in the village. During their detention, Muslim men, women, children, and elderly were kept in harsh conditions, often mistreated or abused. The net result of these actions is hundreds of Muslim civilians leaving the Gornji Vakuf area. If we could have the assistance of the technical booth to show the next video clip, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, among other things in that clip, Your Honours, note that Mr. Praljak said, "I wanted to direction on what to do. I wanted to know what to do in these circumstances." And who did he go to? He went to the minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia and to the president of the Republic of Croatia, Susak and Tudjman respectively. When he needed a decision on what should be done in fighting a battle on the sovereign territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, who did he ask for orders and direction? Susak and Tudjman. Who was directing the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan? Who was telling the Croats what to do and how to go about it? Susak and Tudjman. On the 25th of January, 1993, after the expiration of the HVO ultimatum issued on the 15th, Tudjman specifically stated that Izetbegovic's position on Bosnia's future did not agree with Croatia's state interest or the interests of the Croatian leaders in Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the 9th of February, he went on to say, "The problem was that the Muslims did not agree that Croat authority be established in the provinces designated as Croatian." In other words, the problem is the Muslims aren't going along with it. Susak: "Izetbegovic must turn up with a statement that provinces between Croats and Serbs are indisputable and that must be prerequisite." Now, by this time in Bosnia-Herzegovina there were a number of international organisations and monitoring forces on the ground, including the UN protection force called UNPROFOR, and including such other bodies as the United Nations Military Observers, or UNMOs, are the European Community Monitoring Mission, known as ECMM. They saw and they reported on these developments as they saw them on the ground at that time. In an UNPROFOR report on the 24th of January, 1993, this is what UNPROFOR said about what they saw occurring in Bosnia during this time: "Since the Geneva talks in early January, tensions have suddenly increased between elements of both the Croat HVO and the principally Muslim army of BH in central and southern Bosnia-Herzegovina. "Over the past week -" that is the week prior to the 24th of January - "the political and military leaders of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna have begun to implement their 'understanding' of the proposed settlement. This premature and imperfect grab for control of provinces 3, 8 and 10 has resulted in extremely high tensions and heavy fighting." In a similar report on the 1st of February, 1993, UNPROFOR reported: "The HVO continues to show strong resolution to control the future Croat provinces 8 and 10. Without the prospect of a near-term settlement, the basis for the HVO's assertion of control over proposed provinces 3, 8 and 10 is seriously diminished. Their premature grab for power clearly displayed to all concerned the Croatian Community's intentions." The evidence will show that a number of the accused were directly involved in these events in January 1993, and you've already seen the recording of Mr. Praljak. Likewise, on the 27th of January, Susak reported that he had received updates from Kordic and Stojic on the fighting in Busovaca which included assertions that the Croats had suffered 39 dead and 48 wounded and that the Muslims had amassed 8.500 troops before Busovaca. Susak says: "Praljak and Stojic 'organised everything they could down there in the south.'" Although local cease-fires were declared by late January and early February, Tudjman, Boban and the others had no intention on giving up on the Greater Croatia projects. On the 8th of March Boban said to Tudjman, Susak and a group of Bosnian Croat leaders, "If Bosnia-Herzegovina exists at all we shall have a border. We know exactly how. We have a plan prepared in advance. Herceg-Bosna will never cease to exist. Even within the framework of anything else, there will still be Herceg-Bosna." By February -- by early February of 1993, things had begun to calm down a bit. This fighting in Gornji Vakuf had, under international pressure, had died down and there was a period of a few weeks of what might pass during that time as relative peace. While tensions remained high, there were local skirmishes but no major additional conflicts for several weeks. On the 25th of March, 1993, President Izetbegovic, following further negotiations, provisionally accepted the Vance-Owen Plan, which again the Serbs never accepted, with certain military aspects of the plan still to be resolved. Now, what's important here, Your Honours, what the Prosecution submits is important here is you once again are going to see the exact same pattern of what happened in January. You have talk about a plan being accepted but with conditions and provisions not yet agreed, and the HVO and -- the HVO leadership and those persons, the accused sitting in this courtroom, deciding that, "We're not going to wait for agreement. We're going to enforce this plan whether the Muslims like it or not." By April of 1993, in fact the first few days, Izetbegovic had not made any further agreement, had not resolved additional issues, and there was no final agreement. This is confirmed by a report -- the report of the -- of the peace negotiators to the Secretary-General of the United Nations. If you look at Appendix I, section (e), the section titled "Withdrawal of Forces," what the agreement that Izetbegovic had signed said was: "Both --" not one or the other. "Both Bosnian Muslim army and HVO forces shall be deployed in provinces 5, 8, 9 and 10 under arrangements agreed between them. The process of demilitarisation shall apply to all forces in all these nine provinces and shall be carried out under the supervision of UNPROFOR and in accordance with the detailed arrangements and timetables in the agreement or as negotiated in the military -- Mixed Military Working Group." Again, Mr. President, there was not a final agreement. The Muslims had not agreed to subordinate or withdraw their forces. This was all a matter for further discussion and further negotiation but the HVO would not wait. Tudjman immediately pressed Izetbegovic to sign a statement providing for the HVO's immediate takeover in the so-called Croat provinces. In fact, Tudjman pressed Izetbegovic to meet with Slobodan Praljak to issue a joint statement agreeing to the HVO takeover of the so-called Croat provinces and the removal or subordination of the Muslim army in those provinces. And in fact, once again, the Zagreb Herceg-Bosna leadership acted quickly to enforce their -- [French on English channel]. To enforce their views of the -- [French on English channel]. We're getting mixed translation, Mr. President. Slide 91 -- or the next slide that I will show you, the HVO proposed a 2nd of April, 1993, joint statement for Izetbegovic to sign. This was the language of that statement which you will see in Prosecution Exhibit P1792, and the relevant particular language of the proposed joint statement. However, President Izetbegovic did not sign the joint statement and never agreed to its terms. The top Herceg-Bosna HVO political and military leaders, including some of the accused, were then called to an important special meeting in Mostar on the 3rd of April, 1993, which is also confirmed by adjudicated fact number 155. Adjudicated fact number 155 says -- it's not on the slide. It says on 3 April 1993, the HVO leadership met in Mostar to discuss the implementation of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. The records of that meeting, which we have and which we'll show you, the records of this meeting, chaired by Jadranko Prlic and attended by Mate Boban, Bruno Stojic, and other top officials, made clear both the Croat leadership's plain knowledge, once again, that Izetbegovic and the Muslims had not agreed to the proposed statement and that the Croat leadership clearly intended to go forward with enforcing their position and demands whether Izetbegovic signed or not.
