You'll see in front of you a portion of the records of that meeting. "We hope that Mr. Izetbegovic will sign the document. However, if the joint statement is not implemented, the appropriate military and other authorities of the HVO HZ HB shall implement this provision in regions numbers 3, 8, and 10." At the same time as part of a coordinated approach and a coordinated campaign, at the same time when Jadranko Prlic, Mate Boban, Bruno Stojic and others were meeting in Mostar on the 3rd of April, Mr. Praljak, Slobodan Praljak and Valentin Coric had travelled to Central Bosnia to meet with the HVO leadership in Central Bosnia the day before, on the 2nd of April, 1993. So you can see, Your Honours, the evidence will show you have one group of the Bosnian Croat leadership meeting in Mostar, including some of our accused. We have another set of our accused going to Central Bosnia to meet with the Croat leadership in Central Bosnia. In that meeting in Central Bosnia on the 2nd of April, the records indicate what happened there. Praljak says: "This declaration establishes the immutability of the borders of the Republic of Croatia. The Muslim provinces will be overpopulated. Religious fanaticism will emerge in them. That is inevitable. There will be moving out and resettlement, and the population will homogenise." Then Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, also convicted before this Tribunal, intervened in the meeting, opened the discussion with the other military commanders one of whom asked a question about Vares. General Praljak said: "There is no policy that can enable us to have everything. If you think there is, tell us. The fastest way for Croatia to go down would be to have a state territory extending all way to the Drina. We have never got anything out of that nor ever would. In such a Croatia, around 49 per cent Croats have nothing to seek. This is a classical piece of stupidity. There is no state without a nation. And in that state, where would we be?" "Now, we have got what we want, the homogenisation of our population continues. We can only fence off what is ours and build there our own space and our own state. Territorially speaking, we shall take what continues to be Croatian. What use is a territory where there are no Croats? We need the territory and the borders that we inhabit." And then Kordic goes on to say: "Instructions have also been given to the Croats in Zenica." Essentially they had their opportunity to act, to take control and they didn't do it. "They received their instructions. Now it will be harder for them. Those along the border will be in the Travnik province." The new deadline is now set for the 15th of April, 1993, for the Muslims to comply with the HVO's unilateral plan. Once again, as in January when the deadline passed, the HVO acted immediately, launching a series of attacks all through the territory claimed by Herceg-Bosna, including the massacre and atrocities committed at Ahmici, well known to this Tribunal, on the 16th of April, immediately -- the day after the ultimatum ran, and then in Sovici and Doljani charged in this case on the 17th of April, and in other towns and villages throughout the period, the 17th to the 19th of April. The HVO made a demand. The Muslims didn't comply. The HVO attacked and destroyed and killed. Numerous reports from international observers, including the United Nations, UNPROFOR and ECMM made it abundantly clear that the HVO attacks and war crimes committed in Central Bosnia and Herzegovina during this time were a continuing part of the Herceg-Bosna HVO efforts to implement their view of Vance-Owen. You see in front of you a portion of an ECMM report on the 18th of April. "With both the Bosnian Muslims and Croats signed up to the peace plan but the Croats are now demanding that the Muslims turn control of the Croat provinces over to them. This was to include the removal of BiH army elements or to put them under command of the Croats. Of course, this is totally unacceptable to the Muslims." Another ECMM report of this type a few weeks later is similar. A report written by the head of the ECMM mission in Central Bosnia says: "The latest meeting of the authorities of Herceg-Bosna in Citluk on the 30th of April, 1993, has revealed the political side of the last military events. And it is time now, or never, to express the common, clear feeling of the 23 ECMM monitors of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Bosnian Croats continue to complain that they are attacked by the Muslim forces on all fronts, despite the evidence that they are entirely responsible for the opening of the conflict on the 14th of April and, largely, for its continuation. The fighting began without doubt on the initiative of the HVO, claiming that it was only answering a systematic anti-Croat attitude. It was obviously an attempt to secure and -- to seize and secure the 'Croat provinces.'" The Chamber will hear fairly extensive evidence in the case, the Prosecution case about crimes committed in Sovici, in Doljani, in Prozor and other parts of the so-called Herceg-Bosna in the middle and second half of April of 1993 in connection with these events. Following the Herceg-Bosna attacks, arrests and expulsions in the second half of April of 1993, things begin to pick up speed, if you will. There was once again -- maybe a few short days when there was some hope, some short and unfortunately hollow hope that peace could be obtained, but only a few days later in fact the huge conflict and problems besieged -- all the problems began in Mostar on the 9th and 10th of May, only a few days later. Indeed, it had become clearer and clearer to Tudjman and the Herceg-Bosna HVO leadership from an early date that a Greater Croatia, now having seen repeatedly that the Muslims were not about to go voluntarily or peacefully, that implementing a Greater Croatia would require military force and violence, expulsions, and population displacements. Even as early as January of 1992, you will recall the conversations between Koljevic and Tudjman about the leopard spots and about the homogenisation of populations and how previous historical problems had been solved by population exchanges. A similar statement was made by Tudjman on the 21st of September, 1993: "After World War I a million people were resettled between Greece and Turkey until 1920 and even later. After World War II, 12 million people in Europe were moved or exiled. Therefore, that terrible war, that tragedy for man, family, certain regions, the greatest tragedy in the sense of demarcation between nations creates even more favourable circumstances for the survival of certain nations in the future." In looking ahead where all this would take the people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Your Honours, during the period now from April 1993 to March 1994, the roughly one-year period, one may consider a high-level report prepared by the European Community Monitoring Mission in June 1993, which aptly summarises what was happening during this period of time. "Relations between Croat and Muslim peoples have deteriorated since January from occasional isolated conflict to the present widespread confrontation. Presently the conflict involves three separate areas: Mostar city, Jablanica/Konjic, and the Travnik to Kiseljak road. In Mostar the HVO are trying to bring the Muslims under total control. The HVO assault is aimed at cleaning all non-Croats from the west bank and eventually moving all Muslims out of the city. The Muslims are now encircled on the east bank without water, electricity or communications. Heavy fighting in Jablanica/Konjic area involves HVO attempts to eliminate Muslim influence in the area. The HVO have suffered losses resulting in withdrawal and loss of influence in both towns. The HVO aims appear to be (a), militarily establish a front line between provinces 8 and 10 and the Muslim province 9; eliminate all Muslim resistance to their plans within provinces 8 and 10; (c), eventually cleanse provinces 8 and 10 of Muslims in pursuit of their dream of Herceg-Bosna; and (d), establish a loose confederation with Croatia in due course." As I said earlier, there was a few days of some peace negotiations and talks involving Franjo Tudjman, Izetbegovic, and others. There were some statements being signed and calls for peace, but it was short-lived. And even a few days later, on the 9th and 10th of May, 1993, the HVO forces attacked the Bosnian Muslims as we just read in Herceg-Bosna's self-declared capital city Mostar. The Herceg-Bosna HVO forces rounded up hundreds if not thousands of Bosnian Muslim men, women, children, and elderly. Large numbers of Muslims were expelled in East Mostar while hundreds of others were detained at the Heliodrom prison. One ECMM report from the 17th of May confirms these events. "The fighting in Mostar began on Sunday, the 9th of May, with an HVO strong attack. Even if the Bosnian Croats claimed that they had been provoked, there is no doubt for all observers - UNPROFOR and ECMM - that the attack was planned, precisely organised and conducted." At the time, the HVO tried to give an excuse, and we may hear at some point in this courtroom how the mass arrest of Muslims was done for their own good, for their own safety. But why was it, Mr. President, that only the Muslims had to be arrested for their own safety? Why was it that the Muslims in one flat were arrested while the Croat next door was not arrested? Why was it only the Muslims had to be protected and not the Croat next-door neighbours? On the 11th of May, 1993, Tudjman met again with senior Croatian government and military officials and confirmed his understanding. Once again confirming his understanding that Izetbegovic had not gone along with the plan. Tudjman: "When the Muslim leadership accepted the Vance-Owen Plan, they did it only formally. Izetbegovic never accepted that Vance-Owen Plan because these provinces should have been Croat." On the 20th of May a similar statement. Tudjman says that he told Izetbegovic: "Croats surely cannot agree to lose some areas that used to be part of the Banovina of Croatia, even though 140 thousands of refugees are accommodated in those provinces out of what number of Muslims is 100 thousands. Croatia as a country cannot accept the change in the demographic structure of those areas." And again note the reference to "the Banovina of Croatia." The expulsion of Muslims in Mostar continued in late May and early into June of 1993 with the later expulsions becoming even more widespread, more systematic, and more violent than the earlier ones. The UN's reaction to the HVO attacks in Mostar was immediate. On the 10th of May, the second day of the attack, the Security Council, recalling its statement earlier on the 21st of April concerning the atrocities and killings that occurred in the April violence, the time in the second half of April after the HVO deadline ultimatum ran in April, noting that its earlier concerns about what happened there in the areas north and west of Sarajevo, including Ahmici, the Security Council expresses its grave concern that the major new military offensive launched by Bosnian Croat paramilitary units in the areas of Mostar, Jablanica, and Dreznica. The Security Council strongly condemns this major military offensive launched by Bosnian Croat paramilitary units. It goes on to indicate that: "The Security Council also expresses its deep concern that the UNPROFOR battalion in the area has been forced under fire to redeploy as a result of this latest offensive and condemns the refusal of Bosnian Croat paramilitary units to allow the presence of United Nations military observers in particular in the city of Mostar. The Security Council calls upon the Republic of Croatia, in accordance with the commitments under the Zagreb agreement of 25 April, to exert all its influence on the Bosnian Croat leadership and military units with a view to ceasing immediately their attacks, particularly in the areas of Mostar, Jablanica and Dreznica." However, the attacks and the actions did not stop, and the expulsions in Mostar continued throughout the month of June 1993, as you will hear evidence. You will hear the victims themselves who will come into this courtroom, Your Honours, and tell you how they were evicted from their homes in June 1993 by HVO soldiers and forces. After the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina attacked an HVO military position just north of Mostar town on the 30th of June, 1993, Jadranko Prlic and Bruno Stojic, two of the accused in this case, issued a proclamation calling to -- calling all Croats essentially to arms, saying that they were threatened with extermination, that the very existence of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina was an extreme and imminent danger and that Mostar was and would remain a Croatian town. Further inflaming, further aggravating, further instigating Muslim persecution, discrimination and violence. On the 2nd of July, 1993, criminal enterprise leader Franjo Tudjman told Susak and others at a meeting in Zagreb that it was: "Important to put pressure on the Muslim units on the Neretva front," the Neretva front being a reference to the Neretva River flowing throw through Herzegovina. In fact, by June and July of 1993, the Herceg-Bosna forces had commence a siege against East Mostar, which continued until April of 1994 and involved continual shelling, sniper fire, blocking of humanitarian aid, and horrible deprivations directed against the Bosnian Muslims in East Mostar. And we will come back to that later when we talk about the Mostar aspects of the case in more detail. The Chamber will hear evidence that at this time by early July 1993, the full expulsion of the Muslims in Herzegovina starts in really full force. In Prozor municipality, in Capljina, in Stolac and Ljubuski, throughout the region, you will see from July and August -- in July and August 1993 massive arrests and expulsions of Muslims by the HVO forces, all in a systematic, well-organised, well-planned, concerted basis. This situation, in fact, just to cut through some of my other notes, and I'll only refer to it quickly for the record and so the Chamber can look at these exhibits in the future, these events are summarised in an ECMM report on the 16th of June, 1993, talking about these events in great detail. I'll just mention down to the second half, point number 12 in that report: "The HVO siege of the Muslim areas in Mostar since early May is designed to force a total surrender, followed by ethnic cleansing. In Croat parts of the city, life has returned to normal and the Croats display a self-confident and brash attitude. The Muslim part of Mostar, representing over 20.000 people, is totally besieged by HVO. There is very little food, no water, and no electricity. It is not known how many refugees are in the city." You will also see at the end of that in item 29 again a reference to the collusion between Croats and Serbs against the Muslims. There is a similar report by a UN Special Rapporteur Mazowiecki who wrote a number of records about what was happening in Bosnia during 1993, late 1992, continued into 1994. Those reports, Your Honours, are extremely informative. You will have those in evidence, and they provide a detailed summary of what happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina during this time. In one such report, on the -- for the 6th of September, 1993, again you will see - I won't take the time to go into it here - a detailed report of what's happening, including the mass arrest, the mass imprisonment of Muslim men in such places as Gabela, Dretelj, Capljina; all places and locations charged in the indictment. I want to briefly touch on, for present purposes, Your Honours, another aspect of ethnic cleansing, one which may come perhaps as even more of a surprise but one that you will hear about in this case, which the Prosecution submits really confirms just how calculated and just how, to use the words of one French diplomat, just how Machiavellian this entire situation really was, and that is what some might call reverse ethnic cleansing, or self-cleansing. Not directed at the Muslims but directed against Bosnian Croats themselves. For you see, Your Honours, removal of Muslims from HVO-controlled or claimed territories was only part of the task in creating a Croat Herceg-Bosna. By a number of means, Croats from other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina were also prodded or "encouraged" to their leave their homes in order to establish or reinforce or consolidate a Croat majority in the municipalities more at the core of the banovina in Herceg-Bosna. Remember again Boban's words "Cleanse the border areas." "Not only do we move Croats and Muslims out, but if we move Croats from other parts of Bosnia in, parts that we know we can't hold, we can't expect to hold onto, but if we move Croats into our area we reinforce our control and our claims on these areas." First it was clear that some municipalities and areas claimed by Herceg-Bosna were more Croat than others, and one again only has to look back at some of the maps we've looked at so far today. Areas that did not even have any claim to having a strong Croat majority or even plurality. A judgement was made or evolved over time that it was ultimately more important to Herceg-Bosna's success to move the Croat population from more marginal areas into the core area where the Croat majority could therefore be consolidated or reinforced. A French diplomat Tebault said it best, "It may sound Machiavellian, but it is only Balkan." You will see that in ECMM report on the 19th of June, 1993. "Some people could wonder how Croats could accept desperate their own people for political purposes. The answer has constantly been given by this RC or ECMM Regional Centre. The Bosnian Croats who have today the power in Mostar as in Zagreb and abroad are the Herzegovinian one having great Herceg-Bosna, all middle Bosnia would have been --" excuse me -- "would have been the best solution for them and it remains their official political line but they are realists and they at least understand that they will never be allowed to take -- to make completely disappear Muslims -- millions of Muslims whatever is their wish and temptation to follow the example of the Serbs. The Vance-Owen Plan with its ethnic mixed provinces did not give enough guarantees for maintaining a Croat domination because the national belonging of the provinces was not secured, and the demography was against the Croats if they had to respect the democratic principles, especially one man one vote. They slowly discovered it and it was a real displeasure for them in their talks with us upon the Vance-Owen Plan implementation." Again, in the next paragraph the ECMM report talks about the need to reinforce the Croat population in Herzegovina, and goes on to talk about that. And then the paragraph with these words: "It seems Machiavellic, but it is only Balkan and everybody who has met regularly the top Bosnian Croat leaders, Boban, Stojic, Kordic, Valenta, in various situations and on various subjects where their paranoia and their extremism were not hidden, can easily believe it." Tudjman himself recognised the benefits to be gained by moving Croats out of their homes even though that would be difficult. On the 6th of November, Tudjman: "Of course it is painful - apart from that, 200.000 Croats have already been driven out of their areas. There will probably be another 100.000 of them. It is awful for them but even, looked at historically, you know, we shall have these 100.000 to 200.000 Croats will firm up the Croatian territory here from Istria to Baranja, you understand, when we finish that and so on. So every bad thing is not just bad but we have to make use of it here." The second reasons for this so-called reverse ethnic cleansing or self-cleansing was a matter of political, military and economic practicalities and as part of the ultimate horse trading, if you will, for the Serbs and the Muslims. Tudjman and the Herceg-Bosna leaders knew that sooner or later they would have to trade some territories off against others in order to maintain the core claims to the banovina territory. Perhaps the best example would be the municipality of Vares which we will come to eventually, and I will show you on the map when we come back to one of the municipality maps. You will see when you look at Vares -- keep in mind, Mr. President and Your, keep in mind the municipality of Vares. The next time we have a map of Herceg-Bosna on the screen, look at the situation concerning Vares. And it basically became known to the Herceg-Bosna leadership that they had very little hope, if any, of holding on to Vares as part of Herceg-Bosna. Third and equally important, relocating Croats from other parts of Bosnia and moving them into houses and flats that have been seized from or abandoned by Muslims families, the very Muslims who had been evicted, the very Muslims that had been expelled from their homes. If you put Croat families, if you put Croat people in those houses, the Muslims can't come back. Tudjman said this again as early as September 1993. Tudjman: "I too have told our people, please settle these refugees in those areas, Tasovici, Stolac, et cetera, to be Croats so that Croatian people are present there," not Muslims but so that the Croat are present there. In the same meeting Tudjman told his Herzegovinian followers not to fall prey "to the idea that the left bank of the Neretva River would become part of the Bosnian Republic but do the opposite and 'settle in those areas Ravno, Capljina, Neum and Stolac, and then we shall insist on it.'" Even as late as the 31st of May, 1994 with reference to Croats living in Croat areas and the issues of demographics, Tudjman: "Well, that's clear. Between ourselves it's good that they have stayed down there. I said that there's Ravno, Tasovici, et cetera, and that you should not give territory to the Muslims." Your Honour, that takes us in a broad way through the summer of 1993 and into the fall of 1993, and the problems and the conflict continues, and we will talk about -- the case will tell you about the continued expulsion of Muslims from these areas into the fall of 1993 and the increasing problems with these -- the HVO concentration camps where Muslims were kept under deplorable conditions, and the attacks in Vares and Stupni Do at the end of October 1993. Those will all be features of our case which I will not touch on particularly now in the interest of time. What's the result of all this? What happened as a result of these systematic and well-orchestrated campaigns by the Zagreb and Herceg-Bosna leadership against the Muslims? The result was this: The Bosnian Muslim population in many parts of Herceg-Bosna was substantially reduced if not eliminated altogether. And those who did remain, those Muslims who for whatever reason did remain were plainly dominated by the Herceg-Bosna HVO authorities and forces as planned and intended by the joint criminal enterprise. For example, while in September 1993, there were still 8.000 Muslims in Stolac and 14.000 Muslims in Capljina; by November, just a few weeks later, there were no Muslims in Stolac and only 3.852 in Capljina. The HVO leaders, including the accused, had conducted their work with great efficiency. The full extent and success of their efforts was clearly known to the Herceg-Bosna HVO leadership even much earlier, months earlier. In March 1993, a Bosnian Croat leader bragged to Tudjman, "At the moment there are very few Muslims in Busovaca. Many wished to return but we put Croats in their houses." Likewise in September 1993, the Bosnian Croat leader Markovic informed Tudjman, as I mentioned much earlier this afternoon: "Today, there is not a single Muslim in Stolac. We have populated Stolac with our refugees from Bosnia." And how does Tudjman respond? Does he say, "I'm surprised? I'm shocked? How can you say this?" No. Tudjman's response, "I know all that. You're not telling me anything I don't already know." Tudjman goes on to say, "Well, wait, I said the containers too and that too." Markovic: "We have about a hundred cottages. We have already filled the Stolac area to capacity." On March the 1st, running to the end of this period and concluding this overview of the case, by March the 1st of 1994, Franjo Tudjman and the Herceg-Bosna HVO leadership had entered into the Washington Agreement which established the Croat-Muslim federation and ended at least the large-scale open armed conflict between the two sides. So, Mr. President and Your Honours, we're talking about the period of time that we're primarily focusing on here is from the first Prozor conflict in October 1992 but with a view toward all of the events leading up to it, the creation of Herceg-Bosna, the creation -- the taking of all these steps to persecute, control, and dominate the Muslims up to finally the period October of 1992 to early 1994, and then the signing of the Washington Agreement in about March of 1994. To go back to the words, Your Honour, that I mentioned at the beginning of my opening statement, "It is time that we take the opportunity to gather the Croatian people inside the widest possible borders." Followed by the statement, "Today, there is not a single Muslim in Stolac." Followed by Tudjman's response, "I know all that." In those few sentences, in those short statements, Your Honours, you have it all, cause, effect and knowledge. It is time that we take the opportunity; that's the cause and intent. Today there is not a single Muslim in Stolac; that's the effect. Tudjman's statement, "I know all that," that's the knowledge. Mr. President, I'm about to start a different topic, and I don't know what your plans are for taking the next break. I'm happy to proceed either way. I'll either continue, or if you want to take the break now, I'm in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTOINETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. It is now 20 past 5. Let's have a 20-minute break, and we shall resume around 20 to 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you have the floor again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I will now turn for a few minutes to a bit about each of the accused in the case. Because of the constraints of time, I have limited what I've said about -- going to say about each one, but it will provide an overview for Your Honours as we begin the case. Concerning the accused Jadranko Prlic, a quick summary. As indicated on this slide, he was the head of the HVO government at all times most relevant to the indictment, including in his role as a head of the government, including his supervision of the Ministries or departments of defence and the police or ministry of interior. He was a major HVO policy and decision-maker. This is the man who more than any other controlled the levers of government power or what Herceg-Bosna would have called state power. He presided over HVO law making, an apparatus used to persecute and disadvantage Muslims. He was responsible for all authorities involved in and running the prisons, the HVO prisons and concentration camps, responsible for all authorities involved in expulsions, transfers, and deportations, and as you've already seen from some of the evidence we've touched on this afternoon, a participant in high-level meetings with Tudjman and other senior Croat leaders. A little bit more on background. On 15th of May, 1992, Mate Boban appointed Jadranko Prlic as head of the HVO department of finance, and on the 14th of August, 1992, Boban appointed Prlic to the top and most powerful position in the HVO government as president of Herceg-Bosna's supreme executive, administrative and defence body, the HVO. After the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna became the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna in August 1993, Jadranko Prlic's title changed from president to Prime Minister, although it is our submission that his functions remained largely, if not completely, the same. He continued in this position, that is as Prime Minister, throughout the time covered by the indictment. As Mr. Prlic said yesterday, in fact, he'd said he's held about every possible government position you can imagine. I think he said something, if you put the word "former" in front of any title or position -- government title or position, he's held it. That would be him. He was subsequently the vice-president of the government and Defence Minister of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and deputy Prime Minister and Defence Minister of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina from June 1994 to January 1996. He was the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Bosnia-Herzegovina from January 1996 until February 2001. Mr. President, the evidence will show that for most of 1992 and continuing into 1994, Jadranko Prlic was, other than Mate Boban and indeed perhaps even equal to Mate Boban in many respects, the most powerful official in the Herceg-Bosna HVO political and governmental structure. By late 1993, in fact, he effectively eclipsed Mate Boban. Under tremendous international pressure by late 1993, Tudjman had to essentially remove Boban. Some might consider that as a bit of a sacrificial lamb. Something had to be done in the eyes of the international community, and when Boban was removed, Jadranko Prlic became even more powerful than he already was. He had -- he had both de jure and de facto control, power, and substantial influence over the entire Herceg-Bosna HVO government and military. He directed the work of and was responsible for the HVO government including military matters. He approved and signed decisions and decrees that comprise the HVO's official policy, including the policy concerning the Muslims. He had the power to appoint and dismiss in positions of significant authority persons in civilian, military, and judicial organs of Herceg-Bosna and the HVO. He possessed the authority to establish, appoint wardens and close HVO prisons and concentration camps. He was at the top apart again with the possible exception of Mate Boban, Your Honour, he was at the top of the power pyramid. Bruno Stojic. Bruno Stojic was the head of the HVO defence department, including the military police and the military intelligence. He mobilised, organised, and directed and supported HVO armed forces in every respect. His Defence Department was involved in massive crimes, including expulsions, deportation, and forced labour. He was responsible for the HVO military police, which was involved in extensive criminal activity. And had major responsibility for the HVO prisons and concentration camps. A bit more on Mr. Stojic. On or about the 16th of April, 1992, the army of the Republic of Croatia, that is the Croatian army or HV, by its top commanding officer, Bobetko, assigned Stojic as acting officer in charge of logistical support at the Croatian army's forward command post. Now, again note there, not the HVO army but the Croatian army, the army of the Republic of Croatia at their forward command post on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the 3rd of July, 1992, Mate Boban named Bruno Stojic head of the HVO department and then later called Ministry of Defence, and he remained in this position until November 1993. On 16th of December, 1993, Bruno Stojic was named head of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna's office for the production of sales of weapons and military equipment. As head of the Ministry of Defence, Your Honours, he was the most senior political manager and official of the Department of Defence or Ministry of Defence and had extensive involvement in all matters of that department. Slobodan Praljak. I apologise for a technical problem we may have, but I will just tell you. You will see Mr. Praljak was, as you've heard already, in the early summer of 1991, Mr. Praljak joined the army of the Republic of Croatia and by the 3rd of April, 1992, he held the rank of major general in the Croatian army. On about the 14th of March of 1992, Slobodan Praljak became the assistant -- an assistant minister of defence for the Republic of Croatia, working closely with the Minister of Defence Susak. On the 10th of September, 1992, Croatian President Franjo Tudjman appointed Slobodan Praljak to be one of 14 members of the Republic of Croatia's Council of National Defence. He remained in that position until at least 15th of June, 1993. From approximately the 24th of July, 1993, to 9 November, 1993, Slobodan Praljak served as the military head of the Herceg-Bosna armed forces with the title Commander of the Main Staff. The evidence will show that throughout this period Slobodan Praljak served in these various capacities simultaneously as assistant minister of defence and as head of the Croatian HVO armed forces. He served as a principal conduit for orders, communications and instructions from Tudjman and Susak in Zagreb to the Herceg-Bosna HVO leadership in Mostar and Bosnia-Herzegovina. During this period and throughout this period, he played a prominent role in all aspects of the Herceg-Bosna HVO armed forces and operations. Mr. Petkovic was a Croatian army general, professional army officer. He was the top HVO commander for much of the indictment period, and for those months in 1993 when Slobodan Praljak became the senior top -- or senior commander, Mr. Petkovic continued as essentially the number 2 or deputy commander. So at all times relevant to the indictment, Mr. Petkovic was either number 1 or number 2 in the HVO armed forces. He was assigned early in 1992 as -- by Bobetko to the command of the Croatian army's forward command post in Grude, again in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which -- many of which-- many of that forward command post eventually evolved into or became the senior command staff of the HVO armed forces. From April of 1992 until about July of 1993, at the end of July, Mr. Petkovic, as we said, served as the military head of the HVO armed forces, with the title Chief of the HVO Main Staff. As I mentioned a moment ago, when Mr. Praljak became the head, Mr. Petkovic essentially became -- not essentially, he was the deputy or number two commander. In fact, later, on the 26th of April, 1994, Milivoj Petkovic again rose to the number one position and continued in that position until the 5th of August, 1994. The evidence will show that Mr. Petkovic exercised again both de jure and de facto command and control over the Herceg-Bosna armed forces. At times relevant to the indictment he exercised effective control and substantial influence over the HVO forces. He was responsible for the management, organisation, planning, preparation, training, discipline, supply and deployment and operations of the HVO armed forces. He was closely involved in all aspects of military planning and operations, and he issued organisational, strategic, and combat orders. Valentin Coric at all times relevant to the indictment, or until at least November of 1993, was the head of the HVO military police. He directed and was responsible for the HVO military police, and the evidence in this case, Your Honours, will show the HVO military police itself was involved in extensive criminal activity, often being, unfortunately, at the forefront of the criminal activity, including the mass arrest, expulsions, and looting of Muslim property. Also, he had major responsibility for the HVO prisons and concentration camps. Here again in April 1992, Mate Boban appointed Mr. Coric as the deputy for security and commander of the HVO military police. His position was later changed -- the title of his position was later changed to chief of the military police administration, and he continued in this position until approximately the 20th of November of 1993, at which time he was appointed the minister of interior of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Mr. Pusic. Mr. Pusic was a member of the HVO military police and a military police official, again extensively involved in the detention, movement, exchange, and release of Muslim prisoners and detained persons. He was the head -- he was either the head or a member of various HVO services and organisations dealing with the concentration camps. He supervised and approved the use of Muslim prisoners in forced labour. He played an important role in the HVO system for cleansing and deporting Muslims from Herceg-Bosna. A bit more background on Mr. Pusic: In 1992, he became an officer in the HVO military police in Mostar, held a command position in 1993. By an order dated the 22nd of April, 1993, Mr. Coric assigned Berislav Pusic to act on behalf of the HVO military police in exchanging Bosnian Muslim and detainees held by the HVO. On the 11th of May, Bruno Stojic appointed Berislav Pusic as an HVO liaison officer to the UN Protection Force. On the 5th of July, 1993, Jadranko Prlic appointed Berislav Pusic as head of the service for the exchange of prisoners and other persons. On the 6th of August, 1993, Bruno Stojic appointed Berislav Pusic as president of the commission to take charge of all HVO prisons and detention facilities holding prisoners of war and detainees. During 1993, he was also a member of an HVO Commission for Exchange of Prisoners. As a result of these various positions and functions, Your Honours, Mr. Pusic was an important and instrumental official in the Herceg-Bosna HVO system concerning the detention, use, release, exchange, transfer, and deportation of Bosnian Muslims, and the evidence will show that there's hardly any aspect of that that Mr. Pusic was not directly involved in and that he did not, to varying degrees, control and influence. Or, as an example, an Official Note by the Heliodrom warden Stanko Bozic, dated 10 May, 1993, with reference to a decision that "all ethnic Muslim citizens from the right bank of the Neretva were to be quarantined in the central military prison in the Heliodrom. Berislav Pusic, Biljana Nikic, and Marko Bevanda were authorised to release such persons; Berislav Pusic issued an order that persons be released." Another example, this list is indicated here, the ability of Mr. Pusic to order the release and allowed the release of large numbers of persons including in this particular instance individuals at the field hospital who had been taken away from their flats, who had been expelled from their flats on the 11th of May. Another example: Mr. Pusic could give even permission for a Muslim prisoner to be visited by his mother for 15 minutes. Confirmation -- another example: Confirmation of an order by Mr. Pusic to transfer 200 detainees from the central military prison in Heliodrom to the prison in Capljina until further notice. He also had the ability to approve the release or use of Muslim prisoners in illegal and unlawful forced labour. On the 23rd of June, workers, for example, workers were checked out. Ten -- ten prisoners were taken on the approval or authorisation of Mr. Pusic, taken from the Heliodrom. Another document indicating that on the 21st of July, in a report to not only Coric and others -- excuse me, to Coric and others, 38 detainees sent for work on the order of Berislav Pusic have not been returned. Another final example, a report by the Heliodrom prison warden to Bruno Stojic, three of our accused; Bruno Stojic, Valentin Coric, and Berislav Pusic, dated the 5th of July, 1993, reporting that HVO soldiers fired for two hours at buildings holding detainees with no intervention by the military police to stop them. I'd like to show you and discuss for a few moments an organisational chart which, unfortunately, Your Honours, it will be -- it's a bit small for these purposes but we'll provide you a larger hard copy or version of this chart, but will give you some idea of where the various accused in this case fit into the Herceg-Bosna HVO structures. At the top of the chart you will see Mate Boban. Immediately below Mr. Boban you will see Jadranko Prlic as the head of the government and all the executive departments underneath him, including, for example, the economics department, the finance department, the defence department, and Mr. Stojic being the head of that department, the department of the interior, department of justice, department of social welfare. All those departments were directly subordinate to and under the control and authority of Mr. Prlic. Going down that list, as we already mentioned, you see Bruno Stojic as the minister of defence, and you can go down further through the organisational chart. If you follow on down below Mr. Stojic, you'll come to Valentin Coric, who was head of the military police, but in any event, also a subordinate to Mr. Stojic. On the -- on a number of places on the chart -- well, at least two places on this chart you will see Mr. Pusic. You will see him in the Ministry of Defence under the Ministry of Defence as president of the commission for detention centres. You will also see Mr. Pusic in a box over on the left side of the chart which involves various other authorities, agencies and commissions of the HVO governmental structure, in this case showing his involvement in the service for the exchange of prisoners and other persons. As to the accused Petkovic and Praljak, you will see them in the box on the lower right part of the chart in their roles as the overall top commanders, either number one or number two commanders, of the HVO armed forces with essentially two chains of command, if you will, two lines of authority; one leading back to Mate Boban and one working back through the government reporting to Mr. Stojic and being under Mr. Stojic's direction and management and then ultimately back to Mr. Prlic as the president of the government. That will give you, for now at least, an overview of the structure of the government and military and where each of the accused fit into that structure during this time. If we could go to the next slide. A bit more detail on the HVO government, and again essentially you will hear and see documents -- you will hear evidence and you will see documents mentioning the HVO HZ HB. You might -- some people might use the term cabinet or the department -- the government, that is of the -- of the HVO, with again Mr. Prlic being the head of that government and the various department heads reporting to him, including in that box again Mr. Stojic as head of the defence department. You will also see in this chart the relationship between, if you will, the central HVO government and then the municipal governments, the HVO governments that existed in each municipality and the relationship between Mr. Prlic in the central government and these other local or municipal governments. Can we have the next. This chart shows specifically the organisational structure of the HVO armed forces during really all of the most relevant period of the indictment. Again showing Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Praljak at the top of that chart, and then down through the HVO command structure. The HVO operations were essentially -- or armed forces were divided into four operational zones, one for the south-east Herzegovina operative zone, the north-west Herzegovina operative zone, the Central Bosnia zone, and the Bosanski-Posavina zone, which will not really feature in this case. Below, then, in each of the operative zones you have the further structures of military units and formations, including brigade commanders and some -- and others such as -- in some instances there are operations groups, and others, military formations. You also see in this chart down below the operational zone line, if you will, or row, you will see there were certain assets, so-called, or certain operations or functions of the Ministry of Defence or the armed forces that reported and were under the direct control of Petkovic and Praljak but not controlled by the operation zone but directly controlled by the senior HVO commanders, and many of these things will feature in the case. In the next chart you will see the basic so-called -- the operational zones that I've just mentioned, or military districts. So you have, starting with number one, the south-east Herzegovina operational zone, which includes such places as Mostar and Stolac. You have the north-west Herzegovina zone, which is covered by number 2, including such places as Prozor and Gornji Vakuf. You have the number 3 zone or the Central Bosnia zone, which included places like Novi Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca and Kiseljak and Vares. And then you have number 4, the Posavina operation zone up in the top corner of Bosnia, top right-hand corner, if you will, which again doesn't primarily feature in this case, but there you have it. I just might stop here for a moment to say earlier this afternoon I said remember the next map we see of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and remember that we were talking about Vares. You see Vares and Kakanj sticking out there, if you will, by themselves. That goes back to the point, Your Honour, that we made earlier, that it became pretty apparent early on, or at least by mid-1993 that the HVO and Herceg-Bosna authorities had little hope of being able to hold onto that territory indefinitely, and it was far better to move the Croats from there into Herzegovina as opposed to letting them stay out on -- in an area which could not ultimately be held. I anticipate, Your Honours, that in the coming weeks and perhaps as soon as the following speech by Mr. Praljak, or in the assumptions or implications of the Defence questioning of Prosecution witnesses you will hear that these men, these six men, in fact, had no power, had no knowledge of what was happening, or if they did know, that they could not -- somehow they could not do anything about it. In short, that they had then and they have now no responsibility. In saying this or taking such a position, Your Honours, I think they illustrate well what Rudyard Kipling said some years ago: "Power without responsibility, the prerogative of the harlot throughout the ages." That is the power without responsibility; the men who held senior positions with pride of place and prerogative with power but now they want none of that responsibility. I'll stop, Your Honour. I see Mr. Karnavas on his feet, and I will give Your Honour a chance to respond to him, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise for objecting. I normally would not object during an opening, but I think it's improper --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, Mr. Karnavas, you can't make an objection during an opening statement by the Prosecution. When your time comes, the Prosecution is not going to raise any objection. You will have ample time to challenge everything that is being said. So please sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are men, as I've indicated to you this afternoon, these are men who held senior positions in the HVO government. They enjoyed the power that they held at the time, but now, as we submit to you, they do not want to accept the responsibility that was -- that went along with or should have been part of that power and the privileges that they enjoyed. These men were among the most powerful men in the whole Herceg-Bosna project. They had power, plenty of power, and it is now time that they took the responsibility as well. Moving forward, Your Honours, to touch just very briefly on some of the crime base aspects because we won't have time to discuss all these matters in any great detail. But I'd like to mention some of the common features of the crimes charged in the indictment and the conduct that the Chamber will hear evidence about in this case. The evidence will show that on a widespread and systematic basis and in furtherance of a joint criminal enterprise, Jadranko Prlic, Bruno Stojic, Slobodan Praljak, Milivoj Petkovic, Valentin Coric, and Berislav Pusic, together with other leaders and members of the Herceg-Bosna HVO authorities and forces, engaged in the following forms and types of conduct relevant to the indictment: One was the instigation and fomentation of political, ethnic or religious strife, division, and hatred by the use of speeches, propaganda, false information, all directed and intended to foster and create ethnic distrust, ethnic division, and hatred leading to the commission of more serious and terrible crimes that were committed against the Muslims. That's detailed more in our indictment, and I will not go into it now because of the interest of time. A second common feature, the use of force, intimidation and terror, as charged in the indictment. You will hear much evidence about widespread expulsions, the widespread forcible expulsions of people, of Muslims from their homes, widespread stealing and taking of their property, and the terror that was put upon them especially in connection with the siege of East Mostar, the terrible, terrible conditions that existed there in -- in the second half of 1993. Another common feature you will see is the appropriation and destruction of property. From personal property - that is, money, cars, personal property - to homes, businesses, and religious and cultural institutions, including mosques. A further common feature that you will hear about, Your Honours, is detention and imprisonment. The HVO actions and the ethnic cleansing campaigns that they engaged in involved the widespread detention and imprisonment of large numbers, hundreds and thousands of Muslims throughout 1993. You will also hear again about the forcible transfer and deportation of Muslims. Not only did forcible transfer from one place to another in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but you will hear evidence, something we haven't talked about yet today, the deportation of Muslims to third countries and the systems put in place by which even Muslims held in the concentration camps could sometimes be released if they could promise and make arrangements to leave Herceg-Bosna for another country. Of course, these leaders -- these leaders of the HVO leadership did not care as long as they left Herceg-Bosna and didn't come back. Another common feature you will hear is about forced labour, the extensive use of Bosnian Muslim detainees and prisoners in forced labour, often under extremely dangerous conditions, often under exposed-to-combat conditions, carrying sandbags, building fortifications in the midst of combat, carrying ammunition, retrieving bodies during which many Muslim prisoners were either killed or severely wounded. The Chamber will also see in connection with these crimes a certain pattern and practice that was followed, and you will see this over and over again when we look at the crime base and the particular municipalities. It would often follow this pattern: First, most of the Bosnian Muslim military-aged men, including many who had served in the HVO before, were arrested and detained at various HVO prisons and concentration camps. Then with most of the Muslim men effectively out of the picture, the HVO took control of towns and villages and systematically rounded up Bosnian Muslim women, children, and elderly, who were then detained for varying lengths of time and/or transferred to Bosnian-controlled areas or, again, deported to third countries. I would like to focus on this slide that's put up before you now, map number 14, which shows the basic crime base areas in the case, either as places where such things as expulsions, detentions, imprisonment, destruction occurred, or also the various detention facilities and concentration camps that were used to hold people. And you will see that -- I'll just work basically from the upper -- upper right side down through the map. We have Vares, you have Gornji Vakuf, Prozor, Sovici and Doljani, Vojinjo [phoen], Mostar, the Heliodrom camp located just outside Mostar. You have Ljubuski and not only the municipality of Ljubuski but the prison and camp facilities in Ljubuski. You have the Dretelj camp, you have the Gabela camp, and you have crimes committed, expulsion and other crimes committed in Capljina and also in Stolac. Remembering back early this afternoon when we looked at this similar -- a similar map showing these areas of Croatian majority, plurality - again the areas marked in light blue are the areas marked, if you will, hatched areas between the blue and the buff. Note that except for the camps, except for the various HVO detention camps, most of which were located in areas securely controlled by the HVO, that most of the other crime base, with the exception of Vares, happened in areas not having a Croat majority or Croat plurality. Gornji Vakuf. In a -- what -- however we want to describe this colour, buff or light yellow, Gornji Vakuf, Sovici, Doljani, Mostar, Stolac. And when you think about it, Your Honours, the Prosecution submits that's exactly what you would expect because the conflict was in those areas in which the HVO was trying to exert control and discriminate and exert control and ethnic cleansing of the Muslims in these areas. Not in the Croat areas but in the Muslim areas that they claimed. Your Honour, time will not allow me to go through all these crime base areas, the ones that I've just shown you on the map. I can give you some sampling of some of the crimes in some of the areas, and I'm going to try to sort through my notes, if you will, if you allow me, in the next few minutes and just give you a few highlights, if you will. We discussed earlier today the attack on Mostar on the 9th and 10th of May, 1993, the evictions and expulsions that continued throughout May and June of that year, and really the full-scale expulsions and the full-scale siege that occurred in Mostar in approximately early July of 1993 to early 1994. If I could, I would like to show the next -- if I could have the assistance of the technical booth, if they would show the next clip concerning the siege in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "Croatian propaganda echoing over the front line in Mostar, the most vicious theatre of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Since May, Bosnian Croats, aided and abetted by the Croatian government, have been laying siege to about 60.000 people in East Mostar. Almost all of them are Muslims, and they're fighting back hard. "Fatima and Sadem Matcitc, have just been thrown out of their home by Croat gunmen. Mr. Matcitc, who is 72, managed to put on three shirts and to grab two umbrellas as he left. His wife, who is 70, was still in her nightclothes. "Their neighbour, 84-year-old Mrs. Almassa Humow, arrived a few minutes later. Don't sit there, they told her, they could kill you. Even if Ms. Humow still cared, she didn't have the strength to move any further on her own. "She said the Croats had slapped her so hard that her cheek still hurt. The soldiers say they're Bosnians first, Muslims second, but all the suffering is sharpening their Muslim identity. "The Croats hate us because our religion, she said, but for the soldiers it's not a religious matter. It's a question of power, of protecting their own people. People like the women and children expelled from West Mostar. This family were lucky. The Croats were only trying to scare them. "These people are refugees. They live in a ruin, like thousands of others in East Mostar. She can't walk. She lies in stinking clothes on a soaking bed. The civilians do as they're told. Organisation begins at the front line. They've set up forward first aid stations. Nusreta Becic [phoen], who used to be a geologist, is in charge of this one. She was treating one of her neighbours when there was another explosion. Two men had been walking down the street. She slapped the man who was most seriously wounded to try to stop him going into shock. He died. They managed to save the other man. "It gets no better at night. 500 Muslims have just been robbed and thrown out of their homes in West Mostar by the Croats. They had to cross the river Neretva to get to comparative safety on a bridge made of ropes and planks. Croats were shooting at the people they'd just made refugees. They were trying to kill old men and women, mothers and their children. She was so frightened she could barely walk, but she tried to calm her sons. The refugees spent their first night in East Mostar in a bombed-out theatre. They talked of persecution, rape and murder. 'We were driven to a small wood. My sons were pulled out of the car. They were taken into that wood. I was told that their throats with slit. What do I know about politics? I've never thought about it. Tonight the Croat soldiers told me to shut up, to be quiet. That's what I did. I've never done anything to anyone.' "Another woman said that ten men raped her and robbed her before she was expelled. "Luckily, they didn't kill me. Or lucky as far as being killed is concerned, but the rape ... Sometimes my brain simply stops working. I can't get my thoughts together. I'm fighting on my own. It's difficult."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That is an excerpt, Your Honours, of a much longer video, and in the course of the trial we hope to present the entire video to you and you'll see this in part and much, much more. If I can also show you a couple of additional photographs. If we can switch back to the PowerPoint presentation, please. This is an exhibit that will be in the case showing Muslim prisoners being taken to the Heliodrom around the 9th and 10th of May, 1993. You'll notice, of course, the HVO soldiers standing on the left side, armed. Again, Muslims being -- walking, being taken to the Heliodrom to be detained there. Again, Muslim men on their way to the Heliodrom. You can see the Heliodrom in the background at the valley -- on the valley floor, the long line of buildings in the middle of the picture, that is the Heliodrom facility, parts of which were converted into an HVO detention camp which held many hundreds and thousands of Muslim prisoners throughout this period, and these men are being taken to that facility. Your Honour, there is a number of reports that you will see. Of course, the evidence again -- I submit to Your Honours that some of the best evidence you'll receive are the reports from the UNPROFOR units that were in the area and the UN Military Observers, the UNMOs, from the European Community Monitoring Mission, ECMM, and from some other international organisations who were on the ground. These organisations made detailed daily and weekly reports which covered virtually all of the features of the case and will provide the Chamber with much insight into what was happening during those times. And I've just included a few of them here. We won't go into detail because of the time limitations. If we could go to a few additional photographs concerning Mostar. Another aspect of what was happening in Mostar throughout the second half of 1993 was an extensive shelling and sniping campaign. The continuous shelling of East Mostar killed or wounded hundreds of Muslim civilians of both sexes and all ages. Herceg-Bosna and HVO gunfire killed or wounded at least 135 civilians in East Mostar, including women, children, and elderly, and many of these victims are listed in the annex to the indictment. Firemen responding to emergencies, women washing their clothes, family members going out for water, and small children who ventured outside were killed or wounded by HVO snipers. Members of the international organisations themselves were also routinely targeted by HVO fire, and in fact, and sadly, several UN peacekeepers and other international representatives and aid workers were killed or wounded. This picture that's on the display now, a man carrying a bag and two water bottles, going for water and running to avoid sniper fire. Another young man in Mostar running in front of a badly damaged building, shelled building, trying to avoid sniper fire. Next, picture of a woman carrying an injured child in from an ambulance. I'm sure one of the few ambulances that still existed during this time. Victims, including this young, very young person, child, being brought into the hospital in east Mostar. Doctors and nurses trying to give care. No electricity, using candles for light. Next slide, please. Additional victims being carried into the hospital. An injured boy back in a flat. Notice the shell hole immediately above his head in the wall of the flat. Continuous shelling and sniping of the Muslim areas in Mostar, primarily in East Mostar throughout this period. As I said, sniping also extended to the international organisations. The Spanish Battalion, for example, an UNPROFOR unit in this area, reported direct and deliberate sniping at Spanish Battalion units operating in Mostar, noting that in their reports, which you will see, "The HVO is not very happy with the UNPROFOR presence in the city." On the 3rd of November, 1993, a commander of the UN Military Observers once again protested sniping to the HVO main headquarters. "We feel sorry that we are forced to inform you once more about truly deliberate shooting by HVO snipers toward UN Military Observers located on the left bank of the River Neretva in Mostar. This was the fourth confirmed incident within a single week. So we do not believe that it happened by accident or that somebody shot at random. Accuracy and frequency indicate that snipers were shooting in order to kill UN army observers. When the SpaBat, or Spanish Battalion, tried to help, they found themselves exposed to the direct fire of a machine-gun that was shooting upon their transporter." The evidence will show, Your Honour, that in addition to the human casualties, which is certainly the most important by far, but there was also huge property destruction, and the casualties of war economically and again in businesses and the property that were destroyed. A number especially of mosques and religious properties were destroyed which are listed in the indictment and you will see and receive much evidence concerning that. Mosques in particular were intentionally targeted for destruction as symbols of Muslim religion and of Muslim people. On November 9th, 1993, the Herceg-Bosna HVO forces destroyed the Stari Most or the old bridge in Mostar. A truly world class historical site that was another victim of this war. Much of what the Chamber will hear in fact about Mostar has been confirmed as adjudicated facts in other cases. Adjudicated fact number 295: "The population of East Mostar increased after the 29th of June, 1993, from approximately 30.000 to 55.000." Why is that? How under these circumstances could the population so increase? Because at the very time that all this was happening, the sniping, the shelling, the siege, more and more Muslims from elsewhere were being forced into this enclave by the HVO. Which also had the further effect of making conditions even worse. More and more mouths to feed, more and more persons to be the victims of shelling and sniping, and the loss of humanitarian aid. Adjudicated fact number 296: "The humanitarian situation on the eastern side of Mostar was horrific. There was no running water, electricity, and food. The eastern side was completely encircled. The bombardment was constant." Adjudicated fact number 297: "The humanitarian conditions on the east bank of Mostar were appalling. While the Muslim population was swelling due to the intense expulsions from the west bank, water and electricity services were cut off and humanitarian organisations were denied access for weeks. Crucial public services, such as the hospital, were located on the west bank of Mostar and, thus, no longer accessible to the Muslim civilian population." And adjudicated fact number 298: "The siege of East Mostar continued until the beginning of 1994." Mr. President, if I could ask for the Chamber's guidance on this. I would ask the Court's indulgence to allow me to plan the remainder of my time tonight, if I could have one hour tomorrow to finish my comments, but I would like to know what the Chamber's wishes are so I could make my further statements accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott. We had planned that you would finish today and that Mr. Praljak could then take the floor during the entire day tomorrow. Now, if you need an extra hour, this means that Mr. Praljak will also ask for an extra hour. This means that we will have to come back on Friday. The other alternative, we could perhaps hear you until a quarter past seven, if the interpreters agree to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will try to -- I'll try to finish this evening to accommodate the Chamber, but I will cut through a fair amount of material in the interests of time. Obviously, you've only heard about a very small part of the crime base in this case. I took a few minutes to tell you specifically about Mostar, but you also have to -- will consider Prozor, again Gornji Vakuf, Ljubuski, Stolac, Capljina, the Dretelj prison camp, the Gabela prison camp, more on the Heliodrom. All those, of course, will be the subject of extensive evidence that we'll present to you. Perhaps I can point out a few specific items. You can see, Your Honour, that I'm skipping some of the slides, that we're just going past. In particular, in regards to Capljina municipality, Your Honours, just to give you an additional preview of some evidence concerning the expulsions in this municipality in particular, immediately next door to Stolac, which you've already heard a fair amount about, an HVO order from the 4th of August, 1993, this is an order from the HVO command: "Round up the Muslim population from the wider territory in the depth of the area of responsibility. When rounding them up, do not pay attention to age. Gather detained persons in two collection centres. On completion of the task, report to superior command. "5. In case of resistance by them, respond by opening fire from personal weapons," et cetera. These and similar orders throughout the summer and particularly July and August, 1993, you will see repeatedly, leading to the mass arrest of -- and expulsions of Muslim civilians throughout this area. If I could ask for the technical booth to show the next video clip, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "Capljina seems to be getting back to normal, but scratch beneath the surface and everything has changed. One in four of the town's population has left. They didn't choose to go. "Six months ago, Capljina was sealed off by the militia. Street by street, block by block, a quarter of the town's people were loaded into buses and driven away. They were all Muslims. This was the final step in a campaign of persecution which began when Muslim cafes and shops were looted and destroyed. "Herceg-Bosna has not emerged by accident. The setting up of this state is the realisation of a long-term plan. "Today, all the players in the Capljina football team are Croats. They play beneath the Croatian chequerboard flag. The story of how the Serbs carved out their chunk of Bosnia is well known. The Croats have now done the same, but their game plan has been overlooked. "Herceg-Bosna owes its existence to one man, Croatian President Franjo Tudjman. For him, the making of a Croat state on Bosnian land has been a personal obsession, an obsession which drove him to bang the final nail into Bosnia's coffin. Tudjman has built this state on concentration camps, ethnic cleansing, torture, starvation, all executed by his henchman Mate Boban. "In July he abandoned any pretense of supporting a unified Bosnia by calling openly for a carve-up. Peace negotiations are now based on a union of republics or mini states. Tudjman has satisfied his obsession. Next on the agenda, the joining of this part of Bosnia with Croatia."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could focus on just one of the camps in particular, to give the Chamber a bit more of a preview when we talk about the Dretelj camp, one of the five main camps that are charged in the indictment. If we can change back to the PowerPoint presentation, please. An aerial photograph of the Dretelj camp, showing some of the buildings that were used. Some of the bunkers that were used to hold prisoners during 1993. And the interior of one of the bunkers. When they were finally released under great international pressure in the fall of 1993, this is what the Muslim -- many of the Muslim prisoners looked like. Hundreds if not thousands of Muslim men were held in such conditions for much of 1993 the evidence will show. And if I could have the technical booth again switch to the video presentation and show the next clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "Muslim fighters. Now the Croats interred their former comrades. "Responsibility for the camps went right to the top of the Croat government."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The evidence will show that the Granic that was being referred to was Mate Granic who was the foreign minister of the Republic of Croatia at that time who became substantially involved in the efforts to close the concentration camps under great international pressure. Mr. President, Your Honours, we come back again to what I've said several times this afternoon that ties all of this evidence and all of this account together: "It is time that we take the opportunity to gather the Croatian people inside the widest possible borders." "Today, there is not a single Muslim in Stolac." "I know all that." Cause, effect, and knowledge. It's important, Your Honours, to note, and the Prosecution team would like to say to the Chamber at this time that of course persons on all sides - Croat, Muslim, and Serb - committed crimes, horrendous crimes, and persons on all sides - Croat, Muslim, and Serb - were victims. Indeed, while we may hear protest against or accounts concerning Muslim perpetrated crimes and bad acts, it is the Office of the Prosecutor of this institution which has brought indictments against persons from all sides, and it is this Tribunal, this Tribunal, which has convicted persons from all sides - Croat, Muslim, and Serb - of crimes and atrocities. And, Your Honour Mr. President is particularly aware of that from your own recent trial experience. Yes, indeed, crimes were committed on all sides. But what the jurisprudence tells us, and in fact what common sense tells us, quid pro quo and tu quoque are not defences. The fact that one side or one person committed a crime is no excuse, no justification, and no defence whatsoever to another person or side committing a crime. The fact that Muslims committed crimes, the fact that Serbs committed crimes, all of which are undoubtedly true, as established by the judgements of this Tribunal, is no defence, no excuse, no justification for the crimes committed by Croats against the Muslims. Let me also take this opportunity, as I conclude my opening statement today, to make something very clear: Contrary to some reports or allegations that we sometimes hear, this case and the indictment in this case is not against Croatia, and it's not against the Croatian people generally. Those are false statements, and I'm sure said simply for the purpose of media hyperbole. Indeed, as I just indicated, Croatian people suffered greatly during the Balkan wars and the crimes committed against Croats have been and are being addressed by this Tribunal as they should and must. This is not a case against Croatia or Croatian people but against a group, against a movement, against an enterprise of persons which took the wrong direction, which engaged in the wrong policies and the wrong practices and inflicted great harm and suffering on large numbers of people. And those are the people who must be held to account. It was under their direction, under their policies, under their practices, under their strategies, under their Greater Croatia plan that these crimes were committed, crimes that most assuredly must be addressed, must be prosecuted, ever so much as the crimes committed against Croatian people. Indeed, if the Court will allow me, Croatia is a beautiful and dynamic country that wants to move forward, and I for one hope that it succeeds. This is not a case against Croatia or the Croatian people. It's a case against people who did bad things. Further, and also contrary to what has been said, and I think it was said as recently as yesterday in the Pre-Trial Conference, Your Honour, this case is not against and is not an indictment of everyone who was in the HVO. Undoubtedly, and without any dispute, there were people, there were individuals who served in the HVO honourably and who acted properly. And if anyone says that everyone in the HVO was a criminal, that's the nature of our case, that is a false statement and it's a mischaracterisation of the Prosecution case. Another aspect of our case, Your Honour, and I will just touch on it ever so briefly because of the hour, is the aspects of the international armed conflict. I think you've heard a great deal about that today, especially on the -- what you might all the political side. But you will also hear, Your Honours, extensive evidence about the direct participation, about the direct involvement of the Croatian army, the Croatian military in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And you will not only the hear that, but you'll hear about concerted efforts to conceal, to conceal their involvement and to deny their involvement, all of which never went anywhere because everyone knew, including the international community, including the United Nations, which issued report after report, Resolution after Resolution, calling on Croatia to remove its troops from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and yet there were efforts to deny and cover up and conceal that involvement. And you will hear direct evidence about the steps taken to do that, including statements and conversations by Mr. Tudjman, President Tudjman, and others talking about how that cover-up would be conducted. And of course Mr. Tudjman says, "We had to do it under the cover of volunteers. We had to call them volunteers but everyone knows that they were not." And you'll see that evidence and you'll see those transcripts and the direct ordering of Croatian units, and you'll see the orders and you'll hear the evidence of Praljak and others talking about the direct sending of Croatian army units into Bosnia and Herzegovina, and you'll see the orders. Your Honours, I'll make my concluding remarks now. This International Tribunal was established to investigate, prosecute, and hold to account the most responsible senior persons concerning the horrific crimes committed in the former Yugoslavia since 1991, and in this particular case concerning the Croat-Muslim part of that conflict from 1992 to early 1994. In prosecuting the most responsible senior persons, the type of persons who stand before this Court, this Chamber, these are not people who, if you will, did most of the dirty work themselves. These are not the people who pulled the trigger or who poured the petrol on Muslim houses, who put the dynamite in the mosque, but these are the people who set those policies, who set those practices, who were pursuing a Greater Croatia and a Herceg-Bosna that led to all these things happening. That is the nature of the case. And of course you will not expect in that circumstance for there to be evidence that these particular individuals actually lined up a Muslim individual or group and shot them themselves. They had other people doing that, the evidence will show. The orders that they gave, the policies that they established, the practices that they condoned, that is the nature of the case. Each of the accused charged in this indictment plainly fits the standard of a senior responsible person. Each of them was a senior political or military actor in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the HVO. The evidence will show that each of them played a key and essential role or roles in or concerning the commission of the crimes charged in the indictment. Each of them is responsible for unimaginable harm to countless victims. While the victims may be countless, and even sometimes no longer known, they cannot be forgotten and the wrongs done to them cannot go unpunished. In a very real and genuine sense, Your Honours, Mr. President, it is not Ken Scott or Daryl Mundis or this Prosecution team that appears at the bar today. As Robert Jackson said at Nuremberg, the real complaining party at your bar is civilisation itself. To this same end, the writ of civilisation in seeking justice must constantly expand in the areas and persons it reaches. The writ of justice. I'm reminded of that in the words of John F. Kennedy in his inaugural address in 1961. Even those years ago, he said: "To that world assembly of sovereign states, the United Nations, our last best hope in an age when the instruments of war have far out-paced the instruments of peace, we renew our pledge of support to strengthen its shield of the new and the weak and to enlarge the area in which its writ may run." The writ of international justice must run everywhere. Justice must know no bounds. No one must be allowed to act with impunity. The writ of justice must reach every person, every corner, every hiding place. John F. Kennedy also said, in June 1963: "But peace does not mean an absence of disputes. It does not even require that each man love his neighbour. It requires only that they live together in mutual tolerance, submitting their disputes to just and peaceful settlement." Kennedy continued: "So let us persevere. Peace need not be impracticable and war need not be inevitable." What happened here, Mr. President, Your Honours, in the situation and facts related to this case, that is the tragedy and crimes represented by this case, is that these men and their associates, these men now charged and seated before you, did exactly the opposite. They made peace impracticable and war inevitable. They must be held to account, Your Honours, and that's what the Prosecution case will attempt to do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Scott. I had given you some more time. In spite of this, you ended your opening statement at 7.00. Thank you for this. As you know, Mr. Praljak will be free to speak tomorrow. He will have the entire day, the entire court day, from 2.15 until 7.00 p.m., to make his opening statement. Of course, there will be no objections. There is no reason why there should be any objection to what he's about to say. And following Mr. Praljak's opening statement, we shall convene again next week, on Tuesday, to start with the first witness. It is now 7.00. I thank everybody. The hearing stands adjourned. Let's meet again tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 27th day of April, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.
